docs.title: How to cite
docs.text:
If FreqProb contributes to work you publish, please cite the software and the version you used. Results can change between versions (see the Changelog), so the version number is what lets a reader reproduce your numbers. Check it with:

import freqprob

print(freqprob.__version__)

docs.title: DOIs
docs.text:
Every release of FreqProb from 0.8.1 onwards is archived on Zenodo with its own DOI:

  • A specific version: cite the DOI of the release you used, so readers get exactly that code. Version 0.9.0 is 10.5281/zenodo.23938349, and version 0.8.1 is 10.5281/zenodo.23917394. Later versions are listed under "Versions" on the Zenodo record.
  • All versions: 10.5281/zenodo.23917393 always resolves to the latest release. Use it when you refer to FreqProb in general rather than to results from a particular version.

Releases before 0.8.1 have no DOI; cite them by version number and URL.

docs.title: Citing the software
docs.text:
APA

Tresoldi, T. (2026). FreqProb: A Python library for probability smoothing and frequency-based estimation (Version 0.9.0) [Computer software]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23938349

BibTeX (biblatex, or any style that supports @software)

@software{tresoldi_freqprob,
  author  = {Tresoldi, Tiago},
  title   = {{FreqProb}: A {Python} library for probability smoothing and
             frequency-based estimation},
  year    = {2026},
  version = {0.9.0},
  doi     = {10.5281/zenodo.23938349},
  url     = {https://freqprob.tresoldi.org/}
}

BibTeX (classic styles without @software, such as plain or most journal templates)

@misc{tresoldi_freqprob,
  author       = {Tresoldi, Tiago},
  title        = {{FreqProb}: A {Python} library for probability smoothing and
                  frequency-based estimation},
  year         = {2026},
  note         = {Version 0.9.0},
  doi          = {10.5281/zenodo.23938349},
  howpublished = {\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23938349}}
}

Replace the version, year and DOI with those of the release you used. The citation metadata also lives in CITATION.cff; GitHub's Cite this repository button on the repository page builds APA and BibTeX entries from it.

docs.title: Citing the methods
docs.text: FreqProb implements published methods. When a result depends on a specific estimator, such as Simple Good–Turing or the Chao–Shen entropy estimator, cite the method's original paper as well as the software. The References page lists the source for each method and provides them all as a BibTeX file.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
FreqProb implements established methods from the statistics, natural language processing and ecology literatures. This page lists the primary sources for each method, so that work using FreqProb can cite the methods as well as the software. All entries are also available as a BibTeX file: references.bib.

To cite FreqProb itself, see How to cite.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text: All estimators derive from ScoringMethod and share its contract: build from a frequency distribution, call to score. See How estimators work.

docs.title: freqprob.ScoringMethod
docs.text:
ScoringMethod(config: ScoringMethodConfig)

Bases: ABC

Abstract base class for frequency-based probability smoothing methods.

This class provides a unified interface for all probability estimation methods, supporting both regular probabilities and log-probabilities.

The general workflow is to initialize a method with a configuration, fit it to a frequency distribution, and then score individual elements. Given a frequency distribution mapping elements to their observed counts, each method estimates a probability P(w) for every element w. For unobserved elements, methods reserve probability mass to avoid returning zero.

Subclasses must implement _estimate, which returns the probability of each observed element together with the mass reserved for the rest. The method's own parameters are attributes on the estimator; the shared ScoringMethodConfig carries only what every method may need.

Attributes:

Name Type Description config ScoringMethodConfig

Configuration parameters for the method.

name str | None

Human-readable name of the method, or None before it is set.

logprob bool | None

Whether this instance returns log-probabilities.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 3, "banana": 2, "cherry": 1}
>>> scorer = MLE(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> scorer("apple")  # most frequent item
0.5
>>> scorer("unknown")  # unobserved item
0.0

Initialize the scoring method.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default config ScoringMethodConfig

Configuration object containing the method parameters.

required Note

This constructor should typically be called by subclass constructors, not directly by users.

docs.title: revision property
docs.text:
revision: int

Count of how many times this scorer's estimates have changed.

Starts at 0 and increases on every fit and on every streaming update. A caller that caches anything derived from support, unobserved_score, or the scores themselves should record this value alongside the cache and rebuild when it changes.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE
>>> scorer = MLE({"a": 2, "b": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> before = scorer.revision
>>> _ = scorer.fit({"a": 1})
>>> scorer.revision > before
True

docs.title: support
docs.text:
support() -> Collection[Element]

Return the elements this scorer holds an explicit estimate for.

Every other element is scored with unobserved_score. Together with revision, this is what lets a caller build its own index over the scorer without reaching into its internals.

Returns:

Name Type Description Collection[Element]

The elements with an explicit estimate. The result is a read-only

view Collection[Element]

it must not be mutated, and it may become stale once

Collection[Element]

revision changes.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE
>>> scorer = MLE({"a": 2, "b": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> sorted(scorer.support())
['a', 'b']

docs.title: unobserved_score
docs.text:
unobserved_score() -> Probability | LogProbability

Return the score given to every element outside support.

Returns:

Type Description Probability | LogProbability

The reserved probability (or log-probability) for unobserved

Probability | LogProbability

elements.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE
>>> scorer = MLE({"a": 2, "b": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> scorer.unobserved_score()
0.0

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution) -> ScoringMethod

Fit the scoring method to a frequency distribution.

This method trains the scorer on the provided frequency data, computing probability estimates for all observed elements. It resets any prior state so that re-fitting behaves like a fresh fit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping elements to their observed counts.

required

Returns:

Type Description ScoringMethod

This scorer, to allow method chaining.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE
>>> scorer = MLE({}, logprob=False).fit({"a": 2, "b": 1})
>>> scorer("a")
0.6666666666666666

docs.title: save
docs.text:
save(path: str | Path) -> None

Serialize this fitted scorer to a file.

The scorer can be restored later with load, avoiding the cost of re-fitting. Serialization uses pickle.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str | Path

Destination file path.

required

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE
>>> scorer = MLE({"a": 2, "b": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> scorer.save("model.pkl")
>>> restored = MLE.load("model.pkl")
>>> restored("a") == scorer("a")
True

docs.title: load classmethod
docs.text:
load(path: str | Path) -> T

Load a scorer previously written with save.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str | Path

Path to a file created by save.

required

Returns:

Type Description T

The restored scorer.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

Examples:

>>> restored = MLE.load("model.pkl")
>>> restored("a")

docs.title: Smoothing methods
docs.text:
Basic probability scoring methods.

This module implements fundamental probability scoring methods including Uniform, Random, and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). These methods serve as building blocks and baselines for more sophisticated smoothing techniques.

Lidstone family probability scoring methods.

This module implements the Lidstone family of additive smoothing methods, including Lidstone smoothing (with arbitrary gamma), Laplace smoothing (gamma=1), and Expected Likelihood Estimation (gamma=0.5). These methods add virtual counts to observed data to handle the zero probability problem.

Bayesian (Dirichlet-prior) smoothing.

Good-Turing-family smoothing: Witten-Bell discounting and Simple Good-Turing.

Kneser-Ney and Modified Kneser-Ney smoothing.

Absolute-discounting and Pitman-Yor bigram smoothing.

Both methods discount observed bigram counts and interpolate with a lower-order unigram model. Absolute discounting subtracts a fixed amount from every count; Pitman-Yor generalizes it with a second (concentration) parameter and has absolute discounting as its strength = 0 special case.

Katz and Stupid Back-off bigram smoothing.

Both methods score an observed bigram directly and fall back to a lower-order unigram model for unseen bigrams. Katz back-off discounts observed counts with Good-Turing and computes normalized back-off weights so the result is a proper probability distribution; Stupid Back-off skips normalization for speed and returns unnormalized scores.

Interpolated (linear-combination) smoothing.

Certainty-degree probability estimation.

docs.title: Uniform
docs.text:
Uniform(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Uniform probability distribution.

The simplest baseline: assign equal probability to every observed element, ignoring the counts entirely. Useful as a non-informative prior or as a reference point when comparing smoothing methods.

For a vocabulary of size V with reserved mass p0, each observed element gets (1 - p0) / V and any unobserved element gets p0.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts. The counts are ignored; only the number of distinct elements matters.

required unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass p0 for unobserved elements (0.0 <= p0 <= 1.0). Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Counts are ignored, so both observed elements score the same:

>>> uniform = Uniform({"apple": 10, "banana": 1}, unobs_prob=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> uniform("apple")
0.45
>>> uniform("banana")
0.45
>>> uniform("cherry")  # unobserved
0.1
Note

Because it discards frequency information, Uniform is meant as a baseline. Use MLE, Lidstone, or Laplace when counts should matter.

Initialize Uniform distribution.

docs.title: Random
docs.text:
Random(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True, seed: int | None = None)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Random probability distribution.

Assigns pseudo-random probabilities, useful for testing and as a randomized baseline. Each element is given a random count drawn from the observed count range, and those counts are then normalized like MLE. A fixed seed makes the result reproducible.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts. Only the min/max counts are used, to bound the random counts.

required unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass for unobserved elements. Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True seed int | None

Seed for the random number generator, for reproducible results. Defaults to None.

None

Examples:

The probabilities are random but form a valid distribution, and a fixed seed is reproducible:

>>> freqdist = {"apple": 5, "banana": 2, "cherry": 8}
>>> a = Random(freqdist, seed=123, logprob=False)
>>> b = Random(freqdist, seed=123, logprob=False)
>>> a("apple") == b("apple")
True
>>> round(sum(a(e) for e in freqdist), 6)
1.0
Note

Primarily for testing, debugging, and providing a randomized baseline for comparison. It is not a smoothing method in any meaningful sense.

Initialize Random distribution.

docs.title: MLE
docs.text:
MLE(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

Estimates each element's probability as its relative frequency in the observed data — the most intuitive baseline. For counts c_i with total N, each observed element gets (1 - p0) * c_i / N and any unobserved element gets the reserved mass p0 (0.0 by default, i.e. unseen elements score zero).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass p0 for unobserved elements (0.0 <= p0 <= 1.0). Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Probabilities are relative frequencies; unseen elements score zero:

>>> mle = MLE({"apple": 6, "banana": 3, "cherry": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> mle("apple")
0.6
>>> mle("banana")
0.3
>>> mle("unknown")
0.0

Reserving mass for unseen elements rescales the observed ones:

>>> smoothed = MLE({"apple": 6, "banana": 3, "cherry": 1},
...                unobs_prob=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> round(smoothed("apple"), 3)
0.54
>>> smoothed("unknown")
0.1
Note

MLE underlies most smoothing methods but assigns zero probability to unseen events, which is problematic for sparse data. Prefer Laplace, Lidstone, or a more advanced method when unseen elements are likely.

Initialize MLE distribution.

docs.title: Lidstone
docs.text:
Lidstone(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, gamma: float, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Lidstone additive smoothing probability distribution.

Additive smoothing tackles the zero-probability problem by adding a virtual count gamma to every possible element before normalizing. For counts c_i, total N, and B bins, each observed element gets (c_i + gamma) / (N + B * gamma) and any unobserved element gets gamma / (N + B * gamma). This is the posterior mean under a symmetric Dirichlet prior with concentration gamma. Use it when you need a simple, principled way to keep unseen elements from scoring zero, and tune gamma to trade off between staying close to the data (small gamma) and a more uniform distribution (large gamma).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required gamma float

Additive smoothing parameter (gamma >= 0). 1.0 gives Laplace smoothing, 0.5 gives the Jeffreys prior (ELE), and gamma -> 0 approaches MLE.

required bins int | None

Total number of possible elements. If None (the default), uses the support size |V|. A larger bins reserves more mass for unseen elements.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Add-gamma smoothing gives unseen elements non-zero probability:

>>> from freqprob import Lidstone
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 3, "banana": 1}
>>> lidstone = Lidstone(freqdist, gamma=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> round(lidstone("apple"), 3)    # (3+1)/(4+2*1) = 4/6
0.667
>>> round(lidstone("banana"), 3)   # (1+1)/(4+2*1) = 2/6
0.333
>>> round(lidstone("cherry"), 3)   # 1/(4+2*1) = 1/6
0.167

A larger gamma pulls probabilities toward uniform:

>>> smooth = Lidstone(freqdist, gamma=2.0, logprob=False)
>>> smooth("apple")      # (3+2)/(4+2*2) = 5/8
0.625
>>> smooth("cherry")     # 2/(4+2*2) = 2/8
0.25

A larger bins reserves more mass for potential unseen elements:

>>> lidstone_big = Lidstone(freqdist, gamma=1.0, bins=1000, logprob=False)
>>> round(lidstone_big("apple"), 4)    # (3+1)/(4+1000) = 4/1004
0.004
>>> round(lidstone_big("unseen"), 4)   # 1/(4+1000) = 1/1004
0.001
Note

The choice of gamma is a bias-variance tradeoff: small values stay close to MLE (low bias, high variance) while large values approach a uniform distribution (higher bias, lower variance).

Initialize Lidstone smoothing.

docs.title: Laplace
docs.text:
Laplace(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: Lidstone

Laplace (add-one) smoothing probability distribution.

The special case of Lidstone smoothing with gamma = 1.0, also called "add-one smoothing." Each observed element gets (c_i + 1) / (N + B) and any unobserved element gets 1 / (N + B) — i.e. one virtual observation added to every possible element, corresponding to a uniform Dirichlet prior. It is the most common additive smoother: reach for it when you want a simple, reasonable default that never assigns zero probability.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Total number of possible elements. If None (the default), uses the support size |V|.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Add one to every count, then normalize:

>>> from freqprob import Laplace
>>> freqdist = {"red": 3, "blue": 2, "green": 1}
>>> laplace = Laplace(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(laplace("red"), 3)     # (3+1)/(6+3) = 4/9
0.444
>>> round(laplace("blue"), 3)    # (2+1)/(6+3) = 3/9
0.333
>>> round(laplace("yellow"), 3)  # 1/(6+3) = 1/9
0.111

Initialize Laplace smoothing.

docs.title: ELE
docs.text:
ELE(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: Lidstone

Expected Likelihood Estimation probability distribution.

The special case of Lidstone smoothing with gamma = 0.5, corresponding to the Jeffreys prior for multinomial distributions. Each observed element gets (c_i + 0.5) / (N + 0.5 * B) and any unobserved element gets 0.5 / (N + 0.5 * B) — half a virtual observation per element. This is a middle ground between MLE and Laplace: use it when add-one smoothing feels too aggressive but you still want unseen elements handled.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Total number of possible elements. If None (the default), uses the support size |V|.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Add half a count to each element, then normalize:

>>> from freqprob import ELE
>>> freqdist = {"cat": 4, "dog": 2}
>>> ele = ELE(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(ele("cat"), 3)     # (4+0.5)/(6+0.5*2) = 4.5/7
0.643
>>> round(ele("dog"), 3)     # (2+0.5)/(6+0.5*2) = 2.5/7
0.357
>>> round(ele("bird"), 3)    # 0.5/(6+0.5*2) = 0.5/7
0.071
Note

ELE applies less smoothing than Laplace (gamma = 1), so it stays closer to the observed frequencies while still avoiding zero probabilities.

Initialize Expected Likelihood Estimation.

docs.title: Bayesian
docs.text:
Bayesian(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, alpha: float = 1.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Bayesian smoothing with a Dirichlet prior.

Estimates probabilities as the posterior mean under a symmetric Dirichlet prior, adding alpha pseudocounts to each possible outcome. Each observed element gets (c_i + alpha) / (N + V * alpha) and any unobserved element gets alpha / (N + V * alpha), where N is the total count and V the support size. This is numerically identical to Lidstone smoothing with gamma = alpha, but framed so that alpha reads as prior belief: use it when you want a theoretically principled smoother whose strength you can tune from near-MLE (small alpha) to strongly uniform (large alpha).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required alpha float

Dirichlet concentration parameter (alpha > 0). alpha -> 0 approaches MLE, alpha = 1 gives a uniform prior (Laplace smoothing), and alpha > 1 prefers more uniform distributions. Defaults to 1.0.

1.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Bayesian smoothing with a uniform prior (alpha = 1):

>>> from freqprob import Bayesian
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 8, "banana": 4, "cherry": 1}
>>> bayes = Bayesian(freqdist, alpha=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> bayes("apple")     # (8+1)/(13+3*1) = 9/16
0.5625
>>> bayes("banana")    # (4+1)/(13+3*1) = 5/16
0.3125
>>> bayes("unseen")    # 1/(13+3*1) = 1/16
0.0625

A larger alpha smooths more strongly toward uniform:

>>> bayes_smooth = Bayesian(freqdist, alpha=2.0, logprob=False)
>>> round(bayes_smooth("apple"), 3)    # (8+2)/(13+3*2) = 10/19
0.526
>>> round(bayes_smooth("unseen"), 3)   # 2/(13+3*2) = 2/19
0.105

A small alpha stays closer to the observed frequencies:

>>> bayes_minimal = Bayesian(freqdist, alpha=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> round(bayes_minimal("apple"), 3)   # (8+0.1)/(13+3*0.1) = 8.1/13.3
0.609
Note

A positive alpha is required; passing alpha <= 0 raises ValueError. Equivalent to Lidstone with gamma = alpha.

Initialize Bayesian smoothing.

docs.title: WittenBell
docs.text:
WittenBell(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Witten-Bell smoothing.

Reserves probability mass for unseen elements based on how many distinct types were observed, treating each new type as evidence that more unseen types exist. The reserved mass is T / (N + T), where T is the number of observed types and N the total number of observations; the remaining mass is discounted proportionally so all estimates sum to one:

  • p = T / (Z * (N + T)) for an unobserved element, and
  • p = c / (N + T) for an element observed c times.

Useful as a lightweight discounting method when a simple, parameter-free way to handle unseen elements is needed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Optional total number of possible sample bins for the experiment. If None (the default), it defaults to the number of observed types, so the full reserved mass is assigned to a single unseen bin.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities. Counts are corrected to avoid domain errors when taking logarithms.

True

Examples:

Observed elements are scored by relative frequency over N + T, and unseen elements share the reserved mass:

>>> from freqprob import WittenBell
>>> freqdist = {"the": 100, "a": 50, "cat": 3, "dog": 2, "rare": 1}
>>> wb = WittenBell(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(wb("the"), 3)
0.621
>>> round(wb("rare"), 3)
0.006
>>> round(wb("unicorn"), 3)  # unobserved
0.031

Initialize Witten-Bell smoothing.

docs.title: SimpleGoodTuring
docs.text:
SimpleGoodTuring(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, p_value: float = 0.05, default_p0: float | None = None, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True, allow_fail: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Simple Good-Turing smoothing.

Reestimates counts using the frequency of frequencies (how many elements were seen once, twice, and so on), fitting a log-linear model to smooth the tail so that mass can be reserved for unseen elements. This is the practical Gale-Sampson formulation of the Good-Turing method originally developed by Turing and Good, and is a strong general-purpose smoother when the data show a spread of low-frequency counts (many singletons, fewer doubletons, etc.).

This implementation follows those by "maxbane" (2011, https://github.com/maxbane/simplegoodturing/blob/master/sgt.py), Geoffrey Sampson's original C code (1995-2008, https://www.grsampson.net/Resources.html), and the NLTK project (Loper, Bird et al., 2001-2018). Because of minor differences intended to guarantee non-zero probabilities under expected underflow, the reliance on scipy, and the handling of probabilities that are not computable when SGT assumptions are not met, most results will not exactly match the Gale-Sampson "gold standard", though the differences are never expected to be significant.

Note

Since v0.4.0, unseen queries return the per-word probability p0 / (bins - V) rather than the total mass p0, making the method compatible with perplexity calculations and consistent with the other smoothers. Use the total_unseen_mass property to recover p0 (the total mass for all unseen words combined).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required p_value float

The p-value for the confidence interval of the empirical Turing estimate, guiding the choice between the Turing estimate x and the log-linear smoothed value y. Defaults to 0.05 (Sampson's reference implementation), though the authors suggest 0.1.

0.05 default_p0 float | None

Optional probability for unobserved samples (p0) used when no single-count samples are observed. If unspecified, p0 defaults to a Laplace estimate for the current distribution — an intended change from the Gale-Sampson reference.

None bins int | None

Total support size for computing per-word unseen probabilities. If None (the default), uses the heuristic bins = V_observed + N1 where N1 is the number of singletons, assuming about as many unseen types as singletons. Pass an exact support size if known.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities. Counts are corrected to avoid domain errors when taking logarithms.

True allow_fail bool

If True (the default), estimation proceeds even when the essential SGT assumptions are not met (log-linear regression slope > -1.0, or an unobserved count reached before crossing the smoothing threshold), and may yield an unreliable distribution. If False, raise RuntimeWarning in those cases.

True

Examples:

SGT needs a spread of low-frequency counts, so use a Zipfian-ish distribution with several singletons. Observed elements are discounted and unseen elements receive a share of the reserved mass:

>>> from freqprob import SimpleGoodTuring
>>> freqdist = {"a": 10, "b": 5, "c": 4, "d": 3, "e": 2,
...             "f": 2, "g": 1, "h": 1, "i": 1, "j": 1}
>>> sgt = SimpleGoodTuring(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(float(sgt("a")), 3)
0.307
>>> round(float(sgt("g")), 3)  # a singleton
0.025
>>> round(sgt("unknown"), 3)  # per-word unseen probability
0.033
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 3)  # total mass for all unseen words
0.133

Initialize Simple Good-Turing smoothing.

docs.title: total_unseen_mass property
docs.text:
total_unseen_mass: float

Total probability mass reserved for ALL unseen words (p0).

This is the value that Good-Turing actually estimates. The per-word unseen probability returned by __call__() is this value divided by the estimated number of unseen types (bins - V_observed).

Returns:

Type Description float

Total probability mass for all unseen words combined.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import SimpleGoodTuring
>>> freqdist = {"a": 10, "b": 5, "c": 1, "d": 1, "e": 1}
>>> sgt = SimpleGoodTuring(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 3)  # total mass for all unseen words
0.167
>>> round(sgt("unknown"), 3)  # per-word probability for one unseen word
0.056

docs.title: KneserNey
docs.text:
KneserNey(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, discount: float = 0.75, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Kneser-Ney smoothing probability distribution.

One of the most effective smoothing methods for language modeling. It combines absolute discounting with interpolation and, crucially, weights a word by the diversity of contexts it appears in (its continuation probability) rather than its raw frequency. Each observed bigram scores max(c - d, 0) / c(context) + backoff(context) * P_cont(word), and an unseen bigram backs off to backoff(context) * P_cont(word).

This is absolute discounting with the unigram model replaced by the continuation distribution, and it shares the back-off machinery with freqprob.AbsoluteDiscounting accordingly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping bigrams to their observed counts, in the form {(context, word): count}. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required discount float

Absolute discounting parameter 0 < d < 1. Common values are 0.5-0.8. Defaults to 0.75.

0.75 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Observed bigrams are discounted and interpolated with the continuation model, while unseen bigrams back off to it through the context's back-off weight:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> kn = KneserNey(bigram_counts, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> round(kn(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.625

An unseen bigram whose word is known scores through the context's back-off weight rather than a flat average -- here 0.75 * P_cont(dog), since big was only ever followed by one word:

>>> round(kn(("big", "dog")), 3)
0.375

An unseen context falls back to the continuation probability alone:

>>> round(kn(("new_context", "cat")), 3)
0.5
Note

This implementation assumes bigram input. The discount d is typically between 0.5 and 0.8; 0.75 is a robust default. Reliable continuation probabilities require sufficient bigram data. A word that never appears in the data has no continuation probability, so it scores at the floor rather than borrowing an average.

Initialize Kneser-Ney smoothing.

docs.title: ModifiedKneserNey
docs.text:
ModifiedKneserNey(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Modified Kneser-Ney smoothing probability distribution.

An enhanced Kneser-Ney variant that applies a different discount depending on a bigram's count: d1 for singletons, d2 for doubletons, and d3 for counts of three or more. Those discounts are estimated automatically from the data's count-of-counts statistics, which usually makes it more accurate than the fixed-discount version.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping bigrams to their observed counts, in the form {(context, word): count}. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

The discount adapts to each bigram's count, and the score interpolates the discounted estimate with the continuation model:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> mkn = ModifiedKneserNey(bigram_counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(mkn(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.625
>>> round(mkn(("a", "cat")), 3)
0.558
Note

Modified Kneser-Ney is a standard, state-of-the-art classical smoothing method for n-gram language models. Because it estimates its discounts from the data, it is more robust than fixed-discount methods but needs enough varied counts to estimate them reliably.

Initialize Modified Kneser-Ney smoothing.

docs.title: AbsoluteDiscounting
docs.text:
AbsoluteDiscounting(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, discount: float = 0.75, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Absolute-discounting bigram smoothing.

Subtracts a fixed discount d from every observed bigram count and redistributes the freed mass to a lower-order unigram model. For a bigram (context, word) with count c and context total C,

P(word | context) = max(c - d, 0) / C + (d * N1+(context) / C) * P_uni(word)

where N1+(context) is the number of distinct words seen after the context and P_uni is the unigram maximum-likelihood distribution. This is the classic Ney-Essen-Kneser discounting scheme and the foundation Kneser-Ney builds on — the difference is that Kneser-Ney replaces P_uni with a continuation distribution. Reach for absolute discounting when you want simple, well-understood discounting without Kneser-Ney's continuation weighting.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required discount float

Absolute discounting parameter 0 <= d < 1. Common values are 0.5-0.8. Defaults to 0.75.

0.75 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Observed bigrams are discounted and interpolated with the unigram model, while unseen bigrams back off to it:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> ad = AbsoluteDiscounting(bigram_counts, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> round(ad(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.647
>>> round(ad(("a", "cat")), 3)
0.724
>>> round(ad(("big", "dog")), 3)      # unseen word in a known context
0.288
>>> round(ad(("new", "cat")), 3)      # unseen context backs off to unigram
0.615
Note

This implementation assumes bigram input. Unlike Kneser-Ney it uses raw unigram frequencies for the lower-order model, so a frequent word keeps its weight even if it appears in few distinct contexts.

Initialize absolute-discounting smoothing.

docs.title: PitmanYor
docs.text:
PitmanYor(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, discount: float = 0.75, strength: float = 1.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Pitman-Yor process bigram smoothing.

A two-parameter generalization of absolute discounting based on the Pitman-Yor process. With discount d and concentration (strength) theta, an observed bigram (context, word) with count c, context total C, and t distinct words seen after the context scores

P(word | context) = (c - d + (theta + d * t) * P_uni(word)) / (theta + C)

and a word unseen in the context gets (theta + d * t) / (theta + C) * P_uni(word). The concentration theta controls how much mass is reserved for the base distribution independently of the discount: theta = 0 recovers absolute discounting, while larger theta pulls estimates toward the unigram model. Pitman-Yor priors match the power-law behavior of natural language and are the basis of the hierarchical Pitman-Yor language model, which subsumes Kneser-Ney as a special case.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required discount float

Discount parameter 0 <= d < 1. Defaults to 0.75.

0.75 strength float

Concentration parameter theta > -discount. Defaults to 1.0. 0 recovers absolute discounting.

1.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Larger counts still dominate, but the concentration parameter reserves extra mass for the unigram base distribution:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> py = PitmanYor(bigram_counts, discount=0.75, strength=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> round(py(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.643
>>> round(py(("a", "cat")), 3)
0.697
>>> round(py(("big", "dog")), 3)      # unseen word in a known context
0.337
>>> round(py(("new", "cat")), 3)      # unseen context backs off to unigram
0.615
Note

This implementation is a single-level (bigram) Pitman-Yor model using the unigram maximum-likelihood distribution as its base measure and the number of observed types as the table count. It is a practical approximation of the full hierarchical Pitman-Yor process.

Initialize Pitman-Yor smoothing.

docs.title: KatzBackoff
docs.text:
KatzBackoff(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, k: int = 5, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Katz back-off bigram smoothing.

Katz's method discounts observed bigram counts with Good-Turing and redistributes the freed mass to a lower-order unigram model through normalized back-off weights. Following Katz (1987), only counts up to a threshold k are discounted (counts above k are assumed reliable). For a bigram (context, word) with count c and context total C,

P(word | context) = d_c * c / C if c > 0,

P(word | context) = alpha(context) * P_uni(word) otherwise,

where d_c is the Good-Turing discount ratio for count c and alpha(context) is chosen so each context's distribution sums to one. It is one of the classic n-gram smoothing methods and pairs naturally with freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring, which uses the same count-of-counts machinery.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required k int

Good-Turing discounting is applied to counts 1 <= c <= k; larger counts are left undiscounted. Defaults to 5.

5 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Reliable (high) counts are barely discounted, rare counts are discounted more, and unseen bigrams back off to the unigram model:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 4, ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2, ("a", "dog"): 2,
...     ("my", "cat"): 1, ("my", "dog"): 1, ("my", "bird"): 1,
...     ("his", "fish"): 1, ("her", "fish"): 1, ("its", "bird"): 1,
... }
>>> katz = KatzBackoff(bigram_counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(katz(("the", "cat")), 3)    # reliable count, undiscounted
0.571
>>> round(katz(("my", "cat")), 3)     # singleton, Good-Turing discounted
0.222
>>> round(katz(("my", "fish")), 3)    # unseen in context, backs off
0.333
Note

This implementation assumes bigram input. Good-Turing discounting needs a spread of low counts (singletons, doubletons, ...) to estimate discounts; with too few distinct counts some discounts default to 1 (no discounting), leaving little or no mass for unseen bigrams.

Initialize Katz back-off smoothing.

docs.title: StupidBackoff
docs.text:
StupidBackoff(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, alpha: float = 0.4, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Stupid Back-off bigram scoring.

A deliberately simple, unnormalized scheme introduced by Brants et al. (2007) for web-scale language modeling. An observed bigram scores its relative frequency; an unseen bigram scores a fixed weight alpha times the lower-order unigram score:

S(word | context) = c(context, word) / c(context) if observed,

S(word | context) = alpha * P_uni(word) otherwise.

Because it skips the normalization Katz back-off performs, the scores do not form a probability distribution (they do not sum to one), but they are very cheap to compute and work well for ranking when data is plentiful.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required alpha float

Back-off weight applied when falling back to the unigram model. Defaults to 0.4 (the value recommended by Brants et al.).

0.4 logprob bool

Return log-scores if True (the default), otherwise plain scores.

True

Examples:

Observed bigrams score their relative frequency; unseen bigrams are penalized by alpha and scored from the unigram model:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> sb = StupidBackoff(bigram_counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(sb(("the", "cat")), 3)      # 5 / 8
0.625
>>> round(sb(("a", "dog")), 3)        # 1 / 3
0.333
>>> round(sb(("big", "dog")), 3)      # 0.4 * P_uni("dog")
0.154
Note

Stupid Back-off returns scores, not normalized probabilities, so metrics that assume a valid distribution (such as perplexity) are not meaningful here. Use it for ranking and comparison, where only the relative ordering of scores matters.

Initialize Stupid Back-off scoring.

docs.title: Interpolated
docs.text:
Interpolated(high_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, low_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, lambda_weight: float = 0.7, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Linear interpolation smoothing between two frequency distributions.

Blends a higher-order distribution with a lower-order one using a weighted average, lambda_weight * P_high + (1 - lambda_weight) * P_low. This keeps the specificity of the high-order model while borrowing robustness from the smoother low-order model. Two modes are detected automatically from the keys:

  • N-gram interpolation, when the high-order keys are longer tuples than the low-order keys. The lower-order context is taken as the suffix of each high-order n-gram (e.g. bigram (w2, w3) from trigram (w1, w2, w3)).
  • Same-type interpolation, when both distributions share the same key type (strings or equal-length tuples). Keys are matched directly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default high_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Higher-order frequency distribution mapping elements to counts (e.g. trigrams). For n-gram mode its tuple keys must be at least as long as those of low_order_dist.

required low_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Lower-order frequency distribution (e.g. bigrams).

required lambda_weight float

Interpolation weight 0 <= lambda_weight <= 1 for the high-order model. Higher values favor specificity, lower values favor smoothing. Defaults to 0.7.

0.7 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

N-gram interpolation (trigrams backed off to bigrams). The score of ('the', 'big', 'cat') is 0.7 * (3/5) + 0.3 * (5/10), and an unseen trigram backs off to 0.3 * (5/10):

>>> trigrams = {("the", "big", "cat"): 3, ("a", "big", "dog"): 2}
>>> bigrams = {("big", "cat"): 5, ("big", "dog"): 3, ("small", "cat"): 2}
>>> interp = Interpolated(trigrams, bigrams, lambda_weight=0.7, logprob=False)
>>> round(interp(("the", "big", "cat")), 3)
0.57
>>> round(interp(("unseen", "big", "cat")), 3)
0.15

Same-type interpolation between two string distributions. The score of "word1" is 0.6 * (10/15) + 0.4 * (3/10):

>>> model1 = {"word1": 10, "word2": 5}
>>> model2 = {"word1": 3, "word3": 7}
>>> interp = Interpolated(model1, model2, lambda_weight=0.6, logprob=False)
>>> round(interp("word1"), 3)
0.52
>>> round(interp("word2"), 3)
0.2
>>> round(interp("word3"), 3)
0.28
Note

The mode is inferred from the key types, so mixed tuple lengths within a single distribution raise an error. Unseen high-order n-grams back off to the low-order model, and all probabilities are floored at 1e-10 for numerical stability. The weight lambda_weight is best tuned on held-out data.

Initialize Interpolated smoothing.

docs.title: JelinekMercer
docs.text:
JelinekMercer(high_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, low_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, held_out_dist: FrequencyDistribution | None = None, lambda_weight: float = 0.5, em_iterations: int = 10, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: Interpolated

Jelinek-Mercer smoothing with an EM-estimated interpolation weight.

Jelinek-Mercer smoothing linearly interpolates a higher-order model with a lower-order one, exactly as Interpolated does, but chooses the interpolation weight lambda by deleted interpolation: given a held-out distribution, the weight is fitted with the Expectation-Maximization algorithm to maximize the likelihood of that held-out data. Without held-out data it behaves as fixed-weight interpolation using lambda_weight.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default high_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Higher-order frequency distribution (e.g. trigrams).

required low_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Lower-order frequency distribution (e.g. bigrams).

required held_out_dist FrequencyDistribution | None

Optional held-out frequency distribution used to fit lambda by EM. If None (the default), the supplied lambda_weight is used unchanged.

None lambda_weight float

Interpolation weight 0 <= lambda_weight <= 1 for the high-order model. Used directly when there is no held-out data, and as the EM starting point otherwise. Defaults to 0.5.

0.5 em_iterations int

Number of EM iterations when fitting lambda from held-out data (a positive integer). Defaults to 10.

10 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Attributes:

Name Type Description estimated_lambda

The interpolation weight actually used — either the EM-fitted value or lambda_weight when no held-out data was given.

Examples:

With no held-out data the estimated weight is exactly lambda_weight, and scoring matches fixed-weight interpolation:

>>> trigrams = {("the", "big", "cat"): 3, ("a", "big", "dog"): 2}
>>> bigrams = {("big", "cat"): 5, ("big", "dog"): 3}
>>> jm = JelinekMercer(trigrams, bigrams, lambda_weight=0.6, logprob=False)
>>> round(jm.estimated_lambda, 2)
0.6
>>> round(jm(("the", "big", "cat")), 3)   # 0.6 * (3/5) + 0.4 * (5/8)
0.61

Held-out data that the high-order model predicts well pulls the weight up:

>>> held_out = {("the", "big", "cat"): 8, ("a", "big", "dog"): 6}
>>> jm = JelinekMercer(trigrams, bigrams, held_out_dist=held_out, logprob=False)
>>> jm.estimated_lambda > 0.5
True
Note

EM fits a single global lambda (not the per-context bucketed weights of the original Jelinek-Mercer scheme). The held-out data should be disjoint from the training data for the estimate to be meaningful.

Initialize Jelinek-Mercer smoothing, fitting lambda if held-out data is given.

docs.title: CertaintyDegree
docs.text:
CertaintyDegree(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Certainty-degree smoothing.

Reserves probability mass for unseen elements based on the degree of certainty that no unobserved samples remain, derived from the number of observations relative to the support size. As more of the possible bins are observed, the reserved mass shrinks; the remaining mass rescales the Maximum-Likelihood estimate of each observed element.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Optional total number of possible sample bins for the experiment. If None (the default), it defaults to the number of observed types.

None unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass for unobserved states (0.0 <= unobs_prob <= 1.0). Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities. Counts are corrected to avoid domain errors when taking logarithms.

True

Examples:

Observed elements are rescaled by the computed certainty mass, and the remainder is reserved for unseen elements:

>>> from freqprob import CertaintyDegree
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 8, "banana": 4, "cherry": 2, "date": 1}
>>> cd = CertaintyDegree(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(cd("apple"), 3)
0.515
>>> round(cd("date"), 3)
0.064
>>> round(cd("kiwi"), 3)  # unobserved
0.035
Note

This is an experimental distribution under development by Tiago Tresoldi; it should not be used as the sole or main distribution yet.

Initialize Certainty Degree estimation.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Evaluation of fitted models (Evaluating models) and statistics of a sample (Coverage and entropy).

Model-evaluation metrics: perplexity, cross-entropy, KL divergence, entropy.

Alongside the model-scoring metrics, this module provides sample-based estimators that work directly on a frequency distribution: sample_coverage (the Good-Turing estimate of observed mass) and the bias-corrected entropy estimators chao_shen_entropy and nsb_entropy, which correct the downward bias of the naive plug-in entropy when many types are rare or unobserved.

docs.title: perplexity
docs.text:
perplexity(model: ScoringMethod, test_data: Iterable[Element]) -> float

Calculate the perplexity of a model on test data.

docs.title: kl_divergence
docs.text:
kl_divergence(p_model: ScoringMethod, q_model: ScoringMethod, test_data: Iterable[Element]) -> float

Calculate the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two models.

KL divergence measures how much the approximate distribution Q diverges from the reference distribution P: KL(P||Q) = sum_w P(w) log(P(w) / Q(w)), summed over the distinct elements w of test_data (the support to compare the models on; repeated elements are counted once). It is not symmetric: KL(P||Q) != KL(Q||P).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p_model ScoringMethod

The reference probability model P. Must use logprob=True.

required q_model ScoringMethod

The approximate probability model Q. Must use logprob=True.

required test_data Iterable[Element]

Iterable of elements over which to sum the divergence. Duplicates are ignored.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The KL divergence value.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If either model is not configured for log-probabilities.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE, Laplace, kl_divergence
>>> p_model = MLE({"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 1}, logprob=True)
>>> q_model = Laplace({"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 1}, logprob=True)
>>> round(kl_divergence(p_model, q_model, ["a", "b", "c"]), 4)
0.0109

docs.title: sample_coverage
docs.text:
sample_coverage(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution) -> float

Estimate the proportion of total probability mass that was observed.

Uses the Good-Turing estimator of the missing mass: the share of probability belonging to unseen types is approximately N1 / N, where N1 is the number of types seen exactly once (singletons) and N the total number of observations. Coverage is the complement, 1 - N1 / N.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The estimated observed mass, in [0, 1]. Returns 0.0 for an empty

float

distribution.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import sample_coverage
>>> sample_coverage({"a": 10, "b": 5, "c": 3})  # no singletons
1.0
>>> round(sample_coverage({"a": 8, "b": 1, "c": 1}), 3)  # two singletons of 10
0.8

docs.title: chao_shen_entropy
docs.text:
chao_shen_entropy(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution) -> float

Estimate Shannon entropy with the Chao-Shen bias correction.

The naive plug-in entropy underestimates the true entropy when the sample misses probability mass. The Chao-Shen estimator combines Good-Turing coverage adjustment with a Horvitz-Thompson correction for unseen types, which reduces this bias:

H = - sum_i (C p_i) log(C p_i) / (1 - (1 - C p_i) ** N)

where p_i is the relative frequency of type i, C the sample coverage (see sample_coverage), and N the total count.

When every observation is a singleton the Good-Turing coverage is zero and the estimate would collapse to 0. Following Chao and Shen (2003), and reference implementations such as R's entropy::entropy.ChaoShen, the singleton count is then taken as N - 1, which keeps the coverage at 1 / N.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The estimated entropy in nats (natural log). Returns 0.0 for an

float

empty distribution.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import chao_shen_entropy
>>> import math
>>> # Approaches the true entropy of a uniform distribution when well sampled.
>>> round(chao_shen_entropy({"a": 1000, "b": 1000, "c": 1000}), 3)
1.099
>>> round(math.log(3), 3)
1.099

docs.title: nsb_entropy
docs.text:
nsb_entropy(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None) -> float

Estimate Shannon entropy with the Nemenman-Shafee-Bialek estimator.

The NSB estimator is a Bayesian entropy estimator that averages the posterior mean entropy of a symmetric Dirichlet model over its concentration parameter, using a prior chosen so the a priori entropy is (nearly) uniform. It is well suited to the undersampled regime, where the number of possible types is comparable to or larger than the number of observations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

The size of the assumed alphabet (number of possible types), reserving entropy for types that could occur but were not seen. If None (the default), the number of observed types is used, so no unseen types are assumed. Must be at least the number of observed types.

None

Returns:

Type Description float

The estimated entropy in nats (natural log), in [0, log(bins)].

float

Returns 0.0 for an empty distribution or a single possible type.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bins is smaller than the number of observed types.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import nsb_entropy
>>> import math
>>> # Well-sampled uniform distribution approaches log(K).
>>> round(nsb_entropy({"a": 500, "b": 500, "c": 500, "d": 500}), 2)
1.39
>>> round(math.log(4), 2)
1.39

docs.title: Choosing a method
docs.text:
Start from the shape of your data and what you need the estimates for.

Your situation Methods Key parameters Relative frequencies, no smoothing MLE — A simple, robust default that never returns zero Laplace, Lidstone, ELE bins, gamma Smoothing framed as a prior belief Bayesian alpha Heavy-tailed counts with many rare elements SimpleGoodTuring p_value, bins A parameter-free estimate of the unseen mass WittenBell bins n-gram language models KneserNey, ModifiedKneserNey discount Bigram discounting with back-off to unigrams AbsoluteDiscounting, PitmanYor discount, strength Bigram back-off, normalized or fast KatzBackoff, StupidBackoff k, alpha Combining a specific and a general model Interpolated, JelinekMercer lambda_weight Reserving mass by how fully the support is covered (experimental) CertaintyDegree bins A non-informative baseline Uniform, Random —

By data characteristics:

Vocabulary Data A good default Small dense: most elements seen often MLE or Laplace Large sparse: many rare or unseen elements SimpleGoodTuring, or Lidstone with a small gamma Sequence contexts (n-grams) any KneserNey or ModifiedKneserNey Any a trusted background model is available Interpolated

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Know the number of possible elements. The additive methods and Witten–Bell spread the reserved mass over the bins possible elements, and with the default (bins equal to the observed vocabulary) they reserve less than you might expect. See Choose bins.

Prefer Simple Good–Turing for heavy tails. When many elements are seen once or twice, the number of singletons is direct evidence of how much mass is missing, and SGT uses it. It needs a spread of low counts to fit.

Use the n-gram methods for conditional probabilities. Kneser–Ney, absolute discounting and back-off model \(P(\text{word} \mid \text{context})\) from bigram counts. For a flat distribution over n-grams as elements, any of the other methods applies.

Compare on held-out data. The evaluation metrics score each candidate on data it was not fitted to; that, not the shape of the estimates, is the best guide.

The References page gives the published source of each method.

docs.title: One contract for every method
docs.text:
Every estimator is built from a frequency distribution and then called to score an element. That is the whole interface:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = {"the": 30, "cat": 6, "sat": 3, "mat": 1}
>>> mle = freqprob.MLE(counts, logprob=False)
>>> mle("the"), mle("cat")
(0.75, 0.15)

Swapping methods means swapping the constructor; the call site never changes:

>>> laplace = freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=1000, logprob=False)
>>> round(laplace("the"), 4)
0.0298

Each method's own parameters are constructor arguments: bins, gamma, discount and so on. Fitting happens in the constructor; fit(freqdist) refits the same estimator to new counts.

docs.title: The unseen-element problem
docs.text:
A relative frequency gives anything unobserved a probability of exactly zero. That is usually wrong (an element absent from a sample is rarely impossible), and it breaks anything multiplicative: one zero makes the product of probabilities zero, and its logarithm undefined. Smoothing moves a little probability mass from the observed elements to the unseen ones.

>>> mle("mouse")
0.0
>>> round(laplace("mouse"), 4)
0.001

The methods differ in how much mass they move and in how they share it: evenly across all possible elements (additive smoothing), according to how many elements were seen once (Good–Turing), according to the number of distinct elements (Witten–Bell), or, for n-grams, through a lower-order model (Kneser–Ney and back-off). Choosing a method compares them.

docs.title: Log space and logprob
docs.text:
By default, estimators return log-probabilities (logprob=True), because real data multiplies many small probabilities, and products of probabilities underflow to zero. Pass logprob=False for plain probabilities:

>>> import math
>>> logp = freqprob.MLE(counts)  # logprob=True by default
>>> round(logp("the"), 4), round(math.log(0.75), 4)
(-0.2877, -0.2877)

A log-scorer cannot return \(\ln 0\), so an element with no probability scores \(\ln 10^{-10} \approx -23.03\) instead; see Pitfalls.

The evaluation metrics need log-scorers, and Work in log space shows how to combine log-probabilities safely.

docs.title: Batch scoring and the scikit-learn-style API
docs.text:
predict scores many elements at once, and score is an alias for calling the estimator:

>>> mle.predict(["the", "mat", "mouse"])
[0.75, 0.025, 0.0]
>>> mle.score("cat") == mle("cat")
True

For large inputs, Scale to large data describes vectorized, lazy and streaming estimators that keep the same contract.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: This page fixes the notation used across the documentation and the example counts that the method pages share.

docs.title: Counts and probabilities
docs.text:
FreqProb takes a frequency distribution: a mapping from elements to the number of times each was observed. Elements can be strings, numbers, tuples (such as n-grams) or frozensets.

Symbol Meaning \(c(w)\) the count of element \(w\) \(N\) the total count, \(\sum_w c(w)\) \(V\) the number of distinct elements observed (the observed vocabulary) \(B\) the number of possible elements, observed or not (bins) \(N_r\) the number of elements observed exactly \(r\) times ("frequency of frequencies"); \(N_1\) counts the singletons \(P(w)\) the estimated probability of \(w\) \(p_0\) probability mass reserved for elements not observed

Logarithms are natural logarithms, and entropies are in nats.

docs.title: The example counts
docs.text:
The method pages use the same small, Zipf-like distribution: ten words with \(N = 30\), \(V = 10\) and four singletons.

>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> sum(counts.values()), len(counts)
(30, 10)
>>> sum(1 for c in counts.values() if c == 1)
4

The maximum-likelihood estimate is the relative frequency, \(c(w)/N\):

>>> import freqprob
>>> mle = freqprob.MLE(counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(mle("the"), 4), round(mle("dog"), 4), mle("zebra")
(0.3333, 0.0333, 0.0)

Every other method answers the question this leaves open: how much probability should "zebra", never observed, receive, and where should it come from?

docs.title: Bigrams
docs.text:
The n-gram methods (Kneser–Ney, absolute discounting, back-off) take counts of (context, word) pairs and estimate the conditional probability \(P(\text{word} \mid \text{context})\). They use this example:

>>> bigrams = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5,
...     ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1,
...     ("big", "cat"): 1,
...     ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }

For a bigram, \(c(\text{context}, \text{word})\) is its count, \(c(\text{context})\) the total count of the context, and \(N_{1+}(\text{context})\) the number of distinct words seen after it.

docs.title: Unseen elements: per element and in total
docs.text: A method reserves some total mass \(p_0\) for elements it has not observed, and gives each of them a share of it. When the number of possible elements \(B\) is known, an unseen element receives about \(p_0 / (B - V)\). A call to the estimator always returns the per-element probability; Simple Good–Turing also reports the total as total_unseen_mass.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Smoothing is easy to apply and easy to misjudge. This page collects the surprises that come up most often, with the example counts:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)

docs.title: The default bins reserves nothing
docs.text:
The additive methods spread mass over bins possible elements. By default, bins is the number of observed elements, so the smoothed probabilities of the observed elements already sum to one, and every unseen element is scored on top of that:

>>> laplace = freqprob.Laplace(counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(sum(laplace(w) for w in counts), 6), laplace("zebra")
(1.0, 0.025)

Declare the number of possible elements, so that the observed ones give up the mass the unseen ones receive:

>>> laplace = freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=20, logprob=False)
>>> round(sum(laplace(w) for w in counts), 6), laplace("zebra")
(0.8, 0.02)

With bins=20, the ten unseen elements share the remaining \(0.2\). The same applies to Lidstone, ELE and WittenBell; Bayesian always uses the observed vocabulary. See Choose bins.

docs.title: unobs_prob is a per-element score
docs.text:
MLE, Uniform, Random and CertaintyDegree accept unobs_prob, which rescales the observed elements to \(1 - p_0\) and gives each unseen element the score \(p_0\). It is not shared among them:

>>> mle = freqprob.MLE(counts, unobs_prob=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> mle("zebra"), mle("yak")
(0.1, 0.1)

Querying many unseen elements therefore gives a total above one. Use a method that knows the support size when that matters.

docs.title: A log-scorer never returns minus infinity
docs.text:
A log-scorer replaces a probability of zero with the floor \(10^{-10}\), so an element that should be impossible scores about \(-23.03\):

>>> round(freqprob.MLE(counts)("zebra"), 2)
-23.03

This keeps sums of log-probabilities finite, but it also means that a model which gives unseen elements no mass is not rejected outright by the metrics: its perplexity is merely very large.

>>> test = ["the", "cat", "zebra"]
>>> round(freqprob.perplexity(freqprob.MLE(counts), test))
5646
>>> round(freqprob.perplexity(freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=20), test), 2)
12.37

docs.title: Stupid Back-off returns scores, not probabilities
docs.text:
StupidBackoff skips normalization for speed, so its scores need not sum to one over the words of a context:

>>> bigrams = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5,
...     ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1,
...     ("big", "cat"): 1,
...     ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> sb = freqprob.StupidBackoff(bigrams, logprob=False)
>>> round(sb(("big", "cat")) + sb(("big", "dog")), 3)
1.154

Use it for ranking; perplexity and the other metrics assume a probability distribution.

docs.title: The n-gram methods only read bigrams
docs.text:
KneserNey, ModifiedKneserNey, AbsoluteDiscounting, PitmanYor, KatzBackoff and StupidBackoff take (context, word) pairs and ignore other keys. A word never seen in any bigram has no lower-order probability to back off to, so it scores 0 (or the log floor):

>>> freqprob.KneserNey(bigrams, logprob=False)(("the", "fish"))
0.0

Add such words to the training bigrams, or interpolate with a smoothed unigram model, if they must receive probability.

docs.title: Simple Good–Turing needs a spread of low counts
docs.text: SGT fits a line to the frequencies of frequencies \(N_r\). With few distinct counts, or no singletons, the fit is unreliable, and by default SGT proceeds silently. Pass allow_fail=False to raise a RuntimeWarning instead when its assumptions are not met. Its default bins assumes that as many types are unseen as were seen once; pass the true support size when you know it.

docs.title: Random is not smoothing
docs.text: Random assigns reproducible random probabilities, as a control for comparisons. It does not estimate anything from the counts beyond their range.

docs.title: Evaluating models
docs.text:
perplexity, cross_entropy, kl_divergence, model_comparison · need log-scorers

The way to choose between estimators is to ask how well each predicts data it was not fitted to. These metrics score a fitted model on a list of held-out elements. All of them need models built with logprob=True (the default).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For held-out elements \(w_1, \ldots, w_n\) and a model \(P\),

\[ H = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln P(w_i), \qquad \mathrm{PP} = e^{H}. \]

cross_entropy returns \(H\) in nats and perplexity returns \(\mathrm{PP}\): the effective number of equally likely choices the model faces at each element. Lower is better for both. kl_divergence(p, q, elements) is the Kullback–Leibler divergence of \(Q\) from \(P\) over the support formed by the distinct elements given, \(\sum_w P(w) \ln \big(P(w)/Q(w)\big)\); an element listed more than once counts once. model_comparison returns the perplexity and cross-entropy of several models at once.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Fit on the example counts and evaluate on a held-out sample that includes an unseen word:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> held_out = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "rug"]
>>> models = {
...     "laplace": freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=20),
...     "good_turing": freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(counts),
...     "witten_bell": freqprob.WittenBell(counts, bins=20),
... }
>>> report = freqprob.model_comparison(models, held_out)
>>> for name, metrics in report.items():
...     print(name, round(metrics["perplexity"], 2))
laplace 10.12
good_turing 7.73
witten_bell 9.38
>>> round(freqprob.cross_entropy(models["good_turing"], held_out), 3)
2.045

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Hold data out. Evaluated on its own training data, the unsmoothed MLE always wins, because it gives the training data the highest possible likelihood.
  • Unseen elements dominate. One unseen element scored at the log floor of a model that reserves no mass adds about 23 nats to the sum; see Pitfalls.
  • Compare models on the same support. A model that spreads mass over more possible elements gives each a lower probability; compare models with the same bins, or report it.
  • Only for probability models. Stupid Back-off returns unnormalized scores.

kl_divergence(p_model: ScoringMethod, q_model: ScoringMethod, test_data: Iterable[Element]) -> float

Calculate the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two models.

KL divergence measures how much the approximate distribution Q diverges from the reference distribution P: KL(P||Q) = sum_w P(w) log(P(w) / Q(w)), summed over the distinct elements w of test_data (the support to compare the models on; repeated elements are counted once). It is not symmetric: KL(P||Q) != KL(Q||P).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p_model ScoringMethod

The reference probability model P. Must use logprob=True.

required q_model ScoringMethod

The approximate probability model Q. Must use logprob=True.

required test_data Iterable[Element]

Iterable of elements over which to sum the divergence. Duplicates are ignored.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The KL divergence value.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If either model is not configured for log-probabilities.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import MLE, Laplace, kl_divergence
>>> p_model = MLE({"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 1}, logprob=True)
>>> q_model = Laplace({"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 1}, logprob=True)
>>> round(kl_divergence(p_model, q_model, ["a", "b", "c"]), 4)
0.0109

Each model is evaluated on the same test data, producing a nested mapping of model name to its metric values.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default models dict[str, ScoringMethod]

required test_data Iterable[Element]

required

Type Description dict[str, dict[str, float]]

A mapping of each model name to a ``{"perplexity": ..., "cross_entropy":

dict[str, dict[str, float]]

...}`` dictionary.

If any model is not configured for log-probabilities.

>>> from freqprob import MLE, Laplace, model_comparison
>>> models = {
...     "mle": MLE({"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 1}, logprob=True),

docs.title: Coverage and entropy of a sample
docs.text:
sample_coverage, chao_shen_entropy, nsb_entropy · work on counts directly

These functions estimate properties of the population a sample came from, directly from the frequency distribution, without fitting a model: how much of the population's probability the sample has already covered, and the entropy of the population, corrected for the elements the sample missed. They are widely used in ecology (species diversity) and in the information-theoretic measures of ASymCat.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Sample coverage is the Good–Turing estimate of the observed probability mass, the complement of the unseen mass that Simple Good–Turing reserves:

\[ C = 1 - \frac{N_1}{N}. \]

The plug-in entropy \(\hat H = -\sum_w \hat p_w \ln \hat p_w\), with \(\hat p_w = c(w)/N\), underestimates the population entropy when the sample misses elements. The Chao–Shen estimator (Chao & Shen, 2003) scales the relative frequencies by the coverage and corrects each term for the chance that its element was observed at all:

\[ \hat H_{\text{CS}} = -\sum_w \frac{C\hat p_w \ln (C\hat p_w)}{1 - (1 - C\hat p_w)^N}. \]

When every observation is a singleton, \(N_1\) is taken as \(N - 1\), so that \(C\) stays positive. The NSB estimator (Nemenman, Shafee & Bialek, 2002) is a Bayesian estimate that averages the posterior-mean entropy of a Dirichlet model over its concentration, with a prior chosen to be nearly uniform in entropy. bins sets the number of possible elements, reserving entropy for elements that could occur but were not observed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example counts:

>>> import math
>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> round(freqprob.sample_coverage(counts), 4)  # 1 - 4/30
0.8667
>>> n = sum(counts.values())
>>> round(-sum(c / n * math.log(c / n) for c in counts.values()), 3)  # plug-in
1.978
>>> round(freqprob.chao_shen_entropy(counts), 3)
2.22
>>> round(freqprob.nsb_entropy(counts), 3), round(freqprob.nsb_entropy(counts, bins=100), 3)
(2.089, 2.299)

Both corrected estimates exceed the plug-in entropy: with four singletons in 30 observations, the sample has likely missed some words. Allowing for 100 possible words raises the NSB estimate further.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Coverage is a quick diagnostic. Close to 1, the sample has seen almost everything that matters, and smoothing has little to do; far from 1, the choice of smoothing method matters.
  • Chao–Shen needs no parameters and is a good default for undersampled data.
  • NSB uses the support size when it is known, and is well suited to samples smaller than the number of possible elements. It is slower than Chao–Shen.

docs.title: freqprob.sample_coverage
docs.text:
sample_coverage(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution) -> float

Estimate the proportion of total probability mass that was observed.

Uses the Good-Turing estimator of the missing mass: the share of probability belonging to unseen types is approximately N1 / N, where N1 is the number of types seen exactly once (singletons) and N the total number of observations. Coverage is the complement, 1 - N1 / N.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The estimated observed mass, in [0, 1]. Returns 0.0 for an empty

float

distribution.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import sample_coverage
>>> sample_coverage({"a": 10, "b": 5, "c": 3})  # no singletons
1.0
>>> round(sample_coverage({"a": 8, "b": 1, "c": 1}), 3)  # two singletons of 10
0.8

docs.title: freqprob.chao_shen_entropy
docs.text:
chao_shen_entropy(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution) -> float

Estimate Shannon entropy with the Chao-Shen bias correction.

The naive plug-in entropy underestimates the true entropy when the sample misses probability mass. The Chao-Shen estimator combines Good-Turing coverage adjustment with a Horvitz-Thompson correction for unseen types, which reduces this bias:

H = - sum_i (C p_i) log(C p_i) / (1 - (1 - C p_i) ** N)

where p_i is the relative frequency of type i, C the sample coverage (see sample_coverage), and N the total count.

When every observation is a singleton the Good-Turing coverage is zero and the estimate would collapse to 0. Following Chao and Shen (2003), and reference implementations such as R's entropy::entropy.ChaoShen, the singleton count is then taken as N - 1, which keeps the coverage at 1 / N.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The estimated entropy in nats (natural log). Returns 0.0 for an

float

empty distribution.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import chao_shen_entropy
>>> import math
>>> # Approaches the true entropy of a uniform distribution when well sampled.
>>> round(chao_shen_entropy({"a": 1000, "b": 1000, "c": 1000}), 3)
1.099
>>> round(math.log(3), 3)
1.099

docs.title: freqprob.nsb_entropy
docs.text:
nsb_entropy(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None) -> float

Estimate Shannon entropy with the Nemenman-Shafee-Bialek estimator.

The NSB estimator is a Bayesian entropy estimator that averages the posterior mean entropy of a symmetric Dirichlet model over its concentration parameter, using a prior chosen so the a priori entropy is (nearly) uniform. It is well suited to the undersampled regime, where the number of possible types is comparable to or larger than the number of observations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

The size of the assumed alphabet (number of possible types), reserving entropy for types that could occur but were not seen. If None (the default), the number of observed types is used, so no unseen types are assumed. Must be at least the number of observed types.

None

Returns:

Type Description float

The estimated entropy in nats (natural log), in [0, log(bins)].

float

Returns 0.0 for an empty distribution or a single possible type.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bins is smaller than the number of observed types.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import nsb_entropy
>>> import math
>>> # Well-sampled uniform distribution approaches log(K).
>>> round(nsb_entropy({"a": 500, "b": 500, "c": 500, "d": 500}), 2)
1.39
>>> round(math.log(4), 2)
1.39

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
FreqProb supports Python 3.10 to 3.12 and installs from PyPI:

pip install freqprob

It depends only on NumPy and SciPy. The memory extra adds psutil, used by the memory profiling tools in freqprob.performance.profiling:

pip install "freqprob[memory]"

To check the installation and the version:

>>> import freqprob
>>> isinstance(freqprob.__version__, str)
True

Report the version when you cite FreqProb: results can change between versions, as the Changelog and the Migration guide explain.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
To work on FreqProb itself, clone the repository and install it in editable mode with the development tools:

git clone https://github.com/tresoldi/freqprob.git
cd freqprob
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest

Next: the Tutorial.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial goes from raw text to smoothed probabilities, a comparison of methods on held-out data, and estimates for n-grams. It takes about ten minutes, and every example can be pasted into a Python session. The examples use words, but FreqProb works on counts of anything: species, k-mers, categories, events.

docs.title: From counts to probabilities
docs.text:
FreqProb starts from a frequency distribution: a mapping from elements to how often each was observed. word_frequency builds one from a list of tokens:

>>> import freqprob
>>> text = "the cat sat on the mat and the dog sat on the log".split()
>>> counts = freqprob.word_frequency(text)
>>> counts["the"], counts["sat"], len(counts)
(4, 2, 8)

An estimator is built from the counts and then called to score an element:

>>> mle = freqprob.MLE(counts, logprob=False)
>>> mle("the"), mle("cat"), mle("bird")
(0.3076923076923077, 0.07692307692307693, 0.0)

MLE is the relative frequency: "the" is 4 of the 13 words. The unseen "bird" gets probability 0, which is the problem smoothing solves.

docs.title: Smooth the estimate
docs.text:
A smoothing method moves some probability to elements that were not observed. Laplace smoothing adds one pseudo-count to every possible element, so it needs to know how many there are (bins):

>>> laplace = freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=1000, logprob=False)
>>> round(laplace("the"), 5), round(laplace("bird"), 5)
(0.00494, 0.00099)

With 1000 possible words and only 13 observations, add-one smoothing gives almost all the mass to the unseen words. Simple Good–Turing instead estimates the unseen mass from the number of words seen once:

>>> sgt = freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 3)  # 5 singletons in 13 words
0.385
>>> round(sgt("the"), 3)
0.22

The method pages explain each estimator, and Choosing a method compares them.

docs.title: Work in log space
docs.text:
By default, estimators return log-probabilities, so that scores can be added instead of multiplied without underflowing:

>>> log_sgt = freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(counts)  # logprob=True by default
>>> round(log_sgt("the"), 3)
-1.516
>>> round(sum(log_sgt(w) for w in "the cat sat".split()), 3)  # log P(the) + log P(cat) + log P(sat)
-7.059

docs.title: Compare methods on held-out data
docs.text:
To choose a method, score each on data it was not fitted to. Lower perplexity is better:

>>> held_out = "the cat sat on the rug".split()
>>> models = {
...     "laplace": freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=50),
...     "good_turing": freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(counts),
...     "witten_bell": freqprob.WittenBell(counts, bins=50),
... }
>>> for name, metrics in freqprob.model_comparison(models, held_out).items():
...     print(name, round(metrics["perplexity"], 2))
laplace 22.76
good_turing 9.44
witten_bell 13.84

See Evaluating models for the metrics.

docs.title: Estimate n-grams
docs.text:
For sequences, ngram_frequency counts n-grams, and the n-gram methods estimate the probability of a word given its context:

>>> bigrams = freqprob.ngram_frequency(text, 2)
>>> bigrams[("the", "cat")], bigrams[("sat", "on")]
(1, 2)
>>> kn = freqprob.KneserNey(bigrams, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> round(kn(("sat", "on")), 3), round(kn(("the", "mat")), 3)
(0.662, 0.138)

After "sat", "on" always followed, so it keeps most of the mass; after "the", four different words were seen, and "mat" gets a smaller share. See Kneser–Ney.
