docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
Task-oriented guides, each answering one practical question. They assume you have read the Tutorial.

  • Build frequency distributions: from words, n-grams, characters, k-mers and any iterable.
  • Choose bins: the number of possible elements, and why it matters.
  • Work in log space: adding log-probabilities, mixing models with log-sum-exp, and the floor for impossible elements.
  • Scale to large data: streaming updates, vectorized and lazy scoring, compact storage.
  • Save, load and refit: persisting fitted estimators and the scikit-learn-style API.
  • Worked examples by domain: ecology, genomics and categorical data.
  • Plot a smoothed distribution: observed frequencies against smoothed estimates.

docs.title: Build frequency distributions
docs.text: Every estimator takes a frequency distribution: a mapping from elements to counts. Any dict or collections.Counter works. Elements can be strings, numbers, tuples or frozensets.

docs.title: Words
docs.text:
word_frequency counts the words of a list of tokens, or of a string split on whitespace:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = freqprob.word_frequency("the cat sat on the mat")
>>> counts["the"], counts["cat"]
(2, 1)

With normalize=True, it returns relative frequencies instead; estimators expect raw counts.

docs.title: n-grams
docs.text:
generate_ngrams lists the n-grams of a sequence, and ngram_frequency counts them. A list is a sequence of tokens; a string is a sequence of characters:

>>> tokens = "the cat sat on the mat".split()
>>> freqprob.generate_ngrams(tokens, 2)[:3]
[('the', 'cat'), ('cat', 'sat'), ('sat', 'on')]
>>> freqprob.ngram_frequency("banana", 2)
{('b', 'a'): 1, ('a', 'n'): 2, ('n', 'a'): 2}

Bigram counts are the input of the n-gram methods.

docs.title: Anything else
docs.text:
For other data, count with collections.Counter. Here, the 3-mers of a DNA sequence:

>>> from collections import Counter
>>> sequence = "ATGGCATGCA"
>>> kmers = Counter(sequence[i : i + 3] for i in range(len(sequence) - 2))
>>> kmers.most_common(2)
[('ATG', 2), ('GCA', 2)]
>>> freqprob.Laplace(kmers, bins=4**3, logprob=False)("TTT") > 0
True

With pandas, df["column"].value_counts().to_dict() gives the counts of a column.

docs.title: Choose bins
docs.text: bins is the number of possible elements, observed or not: the size of the vocabulary, the number of species in a region, \(4^k\) for DNA k-mers. The additive methods and Witten–Bell share the reserved mass among the bins - V unseen elements, and Simple Good–Turing uses it to divide its unseen mass. It is the most consequential parameter of those methods.

docs.title: When you know the support
docs.text:
Use the true number of possible elements:

>>> import freqprob
>>> kmers = {"ATG": 2, "TGG": 1, "GGC": 1, "GCA": 2, "CAT": 1, "TGC": 1}
>>> model = freqprob.Laplace(kmers, bins=4**3, logprob=False)  # 64 possible 3-mers
>>> round(model("ATG"), 4), round(model("TTT"), 4)
(0.0417, 0.0139)

docs.title: When you do not
docs.text:
Leaving bins at its default (the observed vocabulary) reserves nothing: the observed elements already sum to one, and each unseen element is scored on top (see Pitfalls). Instead:

  • Estimate the support from the data. Simple Good–Turing's default assumes as many unseen elements as singletons, \(V + N_1\), which is a reasonable starting point for any method.
  • Leave headroom. For a vocabulary that keeps growing, 20–50% more than observed is a common rule of thumb.
  • Compare on held-out data. Try a few values and keep the one with the lowest perplexity, comparing models with the same bins.
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> singletons = sum(1 for c in counts.values() if c == 1)
>>> len(counts) + singletons  # V + N1
14

docs.title: How much mass it reserves
docs.text: For additive smoothing with pseudo-count \(\gamma\), the unseen elements receive \((B - V)\gamma / (N + B\gamma)\) in total, which grows towards 1 as \(B\) grows. A very large bins with add-one smoothing can give most of the mass to elements never seen; use a smaller gamma (Lidstone) or Simple Good–Turing then.

docs.title: Worked examples by domain
docs.text: Estimating probabilities from counts, including for what has not been observed, is the same problem in many fields. Each example below is self-contained.

docs.title: Ecology: species abundance and unseen species
docs.text:
Good–Turing estimation was developed for this problem: how much of a population belongs to species not yet seen in a survey.

>>> import freqprob
>>> survey = {
...     "sparrow": 40,
...     "robin": 18,
...     "finch": 12,
...     "hawk": 3,
...     "owl": 2,
...     "crane": 1,
...     "heron": 1,
...     "egret": 1,
... }
>>> round(freqprob.sample_coverage(survey), 3)  # share of individuals from species already seen
0.962
>>> sgt = freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(survey, logprob=False)
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 3)  # chance that the next individual is a new species
0.038
>>> round(freqprob.chao_shen_entropy(survey), 3)  # diversity, corrected for unseen species
1.463

docs.title: Genomics: k-mer frequencies
docs.text:
Count the k-mers of a sequence and smooth over all \(4^k\) possible k-mers, so that absent k-mers keep a non-zero probability:

>>> from collections import Counter
>>> sequence = "ATGGCATGCAATGC"
>>> k = 3
>>> kmers = Counter(sequence[i : i + k] for i in range(len(sequence) - k + 1))
>>> model = freqprob.Lidstone(kmers, gamma=0.5, bins=4**k, logprob=False)
>>> round(model("ATG"), 4), round(model("TTT"), 4)
(0.0795, 0.0114)

docs.title: Categorical data: priors for rare categories
docs.text:
A smoothed category prior keeps a rare or new category from getting probability zero, as for click counts, product categories or the categories of a feature in a classifier:

>>> clicks = {"electronics": 120, "books": 80, "toys": 25, "garden": 5}
>>> prior = freqprob.Laplace(clicks, bins=10, logprob=False)
>>> round(prior("electronics"), 3), round(prior("music"), 4)
(0.504, 0.0042)

docs.title: Text: word and n-gram models
docs.text: See the Tutorial for word counts, held-out evaluation and a bigram model with Kneser–Ney.

docs.title: Work in log space
docs.text: Probabilities of long sequences are products of many small numbers, which underflow to zero in floating point. Log-probabilities add instead, and stay finite. Estimators return log-probabilities by default (logprob=True), and the evaluation metrics require them.

docs.title: Products become sums
docs.text:
>>> import math
>>> probs = [1e-30] * 20
>>> math.prod(probs)
0.0
>>> round(sum(math.log(p) for p in probs), 1)
-1381.6

To score a sequence, add the log-probabilities of its elements:

>>> import freqprob
>>> model = freqprob.Laplace({"the": 3, "cat": 1, "sat": 1}, bins=10)
>>> round(sum(model(w) for w in ["the", "cat", "sat"]), 3)
-5.352

docs.title: Sums need log-sum-exp
docs.text:
Adding probabilities that are stored as logarithms, as when mixing two models, needs a stable log-sum-exp rather than exponentiating first:

>>> from scipy.special import logsumexp
>>> log_a, log_b = -800.0, -801.0
>>> math.exp(log_a)  # underflows
0.0
>>> round(float(logsumexp([log_a, log_b])), 4)  # log(exp(a) + exp(b))
-799.6867

docs.title: The floor for impossible elements
docs.text:
A log-scorer cannot return \(\ln 0 = -\infty\), so elements with no probability score \(\ln 10^{-10} \approx -23.03\). The floor keeps sums finite; see Pitfalls for its effect on the metrics.

>>> round(freqprob.MLE({"a": 1})("b"), 2)
-23.03

docs.title: Save and load
docs.text:
A fitted estimator can be written to a file and restored without refitting. Serialization uses pickle, so only load files you trust:

>>> import freqprob
>>> model = freqprob.Laplace({"a": 5, "b": 3}, bins=100, logprob=False)
>>> model.save("model.pkl")
>>> restored = freqprob.Laplace.load("model.pkl")
>>> restored("a") == model("a")
True

load checks that the file holds an estimator of the class it is called on.

docs.title: Refit
docs.text:
fit refits an estimator to new counts, keeping its parameters, and returns it, so calls can be chained:

>>> model = freqprob.MLE({"a": 3, "b": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> model.fit({"a": 1, "b": 1})("a")
0.5

revision increases at every refit, so code that caches scores can tell when to rebuild them.

docs.title: The scikit-learn-style API
docs.text:
Alongside calling the estimator, score scores one element and predict scores many:

>>> model.score("a") == model("a")
True
>>> model.predict(["a", "b", "c"])
[0.5, 0.5, 0.0]

docs.title: Plot a smoothed distribution
docs.text: Plotting observed relative frequencies against a smoothed estimate shows where a method takes mass from. This example uses the word counts of The Zen of Python, as the figure on the home page does, and matplotlib, which is not a dependency of FreqProb (pip install matplotlib).

docs.title: The counts
docs.text:
>>> import codecs
>>> import contextlib
>>> import io
>>> import re
>>> import freqprob
>>> with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):  # `import this` prints the Zen
...     import this
>>> zen = codecs.decode(this.s, "rot13")
>>> counts = freqprob.word_frequency(re.findall(r"[a-z']+", zen.lower()))
>>> n = sum(counts.values())
>>> n, len(counts), sum(1 for c in counts.values() if c == 1)
(143, 85, 60)
>>> sgt = freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 2)
0.42

With 60 of 85 words seen once, Simple Good–Turing reserves 42% of the mass for words not in the text.

docs.title: The figure
docs.text:
>>> import matplotlib
>>> matplotlib.use("Agg")
>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
>>> top = sorted(counts, key=lambda w: (-counts[w], w))[:11]
>>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5), constrained_layout=True)
>>> _ = ax.bar(top, [counts[w] / n for w in top], color="0.7", label="relative frequency (MLE)")
>>> _ = ax.plot(top, [sgt(w) for w in top], "o-", color="black", label="Simple Good–Turing")
>>> _ = ax.set_ylabel("probability")
>>> _ = ax.legend(frameon=False)
>>> fig.savefig("zen_sgt.png", dpi=150)

The estimates lie below the bars: every observed word gives up some mass to the unseen ones, the rarer words proportionally more. The figure is produced by this code when the documentation is built.

docs.title: Scale to large data
docs.text: The default estimators are in memory and eager, which is fine for most work. For large or streaming data, FreqProb has alternatives with the same call contract. Reach for them when you hit a limit.

docs.title: Streaming updates
docs.text:
StreamingMLE and StreamingLaplace update their counts incrementally, for data that arrives over time or does not fit in memory:

>>> import freqprob
>>> model = freqprob.StreamingMLE(logprob=False)
>>> model.update_batch(["x", "y", "x", "z"])
>>> model("x")
0.5
>>> model.update_single("x")
>>> model("x")
0.6

docs.title: Vectorized scoring
docs.text:
VectorizedScorer scores many elements at once into a NumPy array, which is much faster than a Python loop. BatchScorer does the same for several estimators side by side:

>>> scorer = freqprob.VectorizedScorer(freqprob.MLE({"a": 3, "b": 1}, logprob=False))
>>> scorer.score_batch(["a", "b", "c"]).tolist()
[0.75, 0.25, 0.0]

docs.title: Lazy evaluation
docs.text:
A lazy estimator computes each element's probability only when it is first scored, which helps when only a small part of a large vocabulary is queried:

>>> lazy = freqprob.create_lazy_mle({"a": 3, "b": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> lazy("a")
0.75

docs.title: Compact storage
docs.text:
CompressedFrequencyDistribution and SparseFrequencyDistribution hold large, skewed count tables in less memory, and QuantizedProbabilityTable stores probabilities at reduced precision:

>>> compact = freqprob.CompressedFrequencyDistribution.from_counts({"a": 100, "b": 50, "c": 1})
>>> compact.get_memory_usage()["total"] > 0
True

To measure the difference, freqprob.performance.profiling provides MemoryProfiler and DistributionMemoryAnalyzer. They are development tools, so they are imported from that module rather than from freqprob.

docs.title: Caches

docs.title: Absolute discounting and Pitman–Yor
docs.text:
AbsoluteDiscounting, PitmanYor · n-gram smoothing · bigram input

Absolute discounting (Ney, Essen & Kneser, 1994) subtracts a fixed discount from every observed bigram count and gives the freed mass to a unigram model. It is Kneser–Ney without the continuation counts. The Pitman–Yor estimator adds a concentration parameter, following the Pitman–Yor process (Pitman & Yor, 1997) that underlies hierarchical Bayesian language models (Teh, 2006).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a bigram \((v, w)\) with count \(c(v, w)\) and context total \(c(v)\), absolute discounting with discount \(d\) gives

\[ P(w \mid v) = \frac{\max\big(c(v, w) - d,\ 0\big)}{c(v)} + \frac{d\,N_{1+}(v)}{c(v)}\,P_{\text{uni}}(w), \]

where \(P_{\text{uni}}\) is the relative frequency of \(w\) as the second element of a bigram. With concentration \(\theta\) = strength and \(t = N_{1+}(v)\), Pitman–Yor gives

\[ P(w \mid v) = \frac{\max\big(c(v, w) - d,\ 0\big) + (\theta + d\,t)\,P_{\text{uni}}(w)}{\theta + c(v)}, \]

which is absolute discounting when \(\theta = 0\). Unseen contexts back off to \(P_{\text{uni}}(w)\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example bigrams:

>>> import freqprob
>>> bigrams = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5,
...     ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1,
...     ("big", "cat"): 1,
...     ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> queries = [("the", "cat"), ("big", "dog"), ("new", "cat")]
>>> ad = freqprob.AbsoluteDiscounting(bigrams, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> [round(ad(b), 3) for b in queries]
[0.647, 0.288, 0.615]
>>> py = freqprob.PitmanYor(bigrams, discount=0.75, strength=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> [round(py(b), 3) for b in queries]
[0.643, 0.337, 0.615]

"cat" is the more frequent word (\(8/13\)), so unlike under Kneser–Ney it keeps that weight in a new context. The concentration parameter moves more mass to the unigram model: "dog" after "big" rises from 0.288 to 0.337.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Normalized over the words of each context.
  • Uses raw unigram frequencies for the back-off, so a frequent word keeps its weight even if it occurs in few contexts; Kneser–Ney corrects this.
  • strength controls the mass given to the unigram model independently of the discount; it must exceed \(-d\).
  • Bigrams only, as for Kneser–Ney.

docs.title: freqprob.AbsoluteDiscounting
docs.text:
AbsoluteDiscounting(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, discount: float = 0.75, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Absolute-discounting bigram smoothing.

Subtracts a fixed discount d from every observed bigram count and redistributes the freed mass to a lower-order unigram model. For a bigram (context, word) with count c and context total C,

P(word | context) = max(c - d, 0) / C + (d * N1+(context) / C) * P_uni(word)

where N1+(context) is the number of distinct words seen after the context and P_uni is the unigram maximum-likelihood distribution. This is the classic Ney-Essen-Kneser discounting scheme and the foundation Kneser-Ney builds on — the difference is that Kneser-Ney replaces P_uni with a continuation distribution. Reach for absolute discounting when you want simple, well-understood discounting without Kneser-Ney's continuation weighting.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required discount float

Absolute discounting parameter 0 <= d < 1. Common values are 0.5-0.8. Defaults to 0.75.

0.75 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Observed bigrams are discounted and interpolated with the unigram model, while unseen bigrams back off to it:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> ad = AbsoluteDiscounting(bigram_counts, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> round(ad(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.647
>>> round(ad(("a", "cat")), 3)
0.724
>>> round(ad(("big", "dog")), 3)      # unseen word in a known context
0.288
>>> round(ad(("new", "cat")), 3)      # unseen context backs off to unigram
0.615
Note

This implementation assumes bigram input. Unlike Kneser-Ney it uses raw unigram frequencies for the lower-order model, so a frequent word keeps its weight even if it appears in few distinct contexts.

docs.title: freqprob.PitmanYor
docs.text:
PitmanYor(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, discount: float = 0.75, strength: float = 1.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Pitman-Yor process bigram smoothing.

A two-parameter generalization of absolute discounting based on the Pitman-Yor process. With discount d and concentration (strength) theta, an observed bigram (context, word) with count c, context total C, and t distinct words seen after the context scores

P(word | context) = (c - d + (theta + d * t) * P_uni(word)) / (theta + C)

and a word unseen in the context gets (theta + d * t) / (theta + C) * P_uni(word). The concentration theta controls how much mass is reserved for the base distribution independently of the discount: theta = 0 recovers absolute discounting, while larger theta pulls estimates toward the unigram model. Pitman-Yor priors match the power-law behavior of natural language and are the basis of the hierarchical Pitman-Yor language model, which subsumes Kneser-Ney as a special case.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required discount float

Discount parameter 0 <= d < 1. Defaults to 0.75.

0.75 strength float

Concentration parameter theta > -discount. Defaults to 1.0. 0 recovers absolute discounting.

1.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Larger counts still dominate, but the concentration parameter reserves extra mass for the unigram base distribution:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> py = PitmanYor(bigram_counts, discount=0.75, strength=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> round(py(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.643
>>> round(py(("a", "cat")), 3)
0.697
>>> round(py(("big", "dog")), 3)      # unseen word in a known context
0.337
>>> round(py(("new", "cat")), 3)      # unseen context backs off to unigram
0.615
Note

This implementation is a single-level (bigram) Pitman-Yor model using the unigram maximum-likelihood distribution as its base measure and the number of observed types as the table count. It is a practical approximation of the full hierarchical Pitman-Yor process.

docs.text: • Ney, Essen & Kneser (1994); Pitman & Yor (1997); Teh (2006). See References.

docs.title: Additive smoothing: Laplace, Lidstone, ELE, Bayesian
docs.text:
Lidstone, Laplace, ELE, Bayesian · additive smoothing

Additive smoothing adds a pseudo-count to every possible element before normalizing, so that no element has probability zero. It is the oldest and simplest form of smoothing (Laplace's rule of succession), and a robust default when the number of possible elements is known.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With pseudo-count \(\gamma\) and \(B\) possible elements (bins),

\[ P(w) = \frac{c(w) + \gamma}{N + B\gamma}, \qquad P(\text{unseen}) = \frac{\gamma}{N + B\gamma}. \] Estimator \(\gamma\) Lidstone(counts, gamma, bins) any \(\gamma \geq 0\) Laplace(counts, bins) 1 ("add one") ELE(counts, bins) 0.5 (the expected likelihood estimate; Jeffreys' prior)

This is the posterior mean of a multinomial under a symmetric Dirichlet prior with concentration \(\gamma\). bins defaults to the observed vocabulary \(V\); see the properties below.

docs.title: Bayesian smoothing
docs.text: Bayesian(counts, alpha) computes the same estimate with \(\gamma = \alpha\) and \(B = V\), framing \(\alpha\) as the strength of a Dirichlet prior. It has no bins argument.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example counts and a support of 100 possible words:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> for name, model in [
...     ("Laplace", freqprob.Laplace(counts, bins=100, logprob=False)),
...     ("ELE", freqprob.ELE(counts, bins=100, logprob=False)),
...     ("Lidstone 0.1", freqprob.Lidstone(counts, gamma=0.1, bins=100, logprob=False)),
... ]:
...     print(name, [round(model(w), 4) for w in ("the", "dog", "zebra")])
Laplace [0.0846, 0.0154, 0.0077]
ELE [0.1313, 0.0187, 0.0063]
Lidstone 0.1 [0.2525, 0.0275, 0.0025]

With 30 observations and 100 possible words, add-one smoothing gives the 90 unseen words \(90/130 \approx 69\%\) of the mass, and the most frequent word falls from \(1/3\) to \(0.085\). A smaller \(\gamma\) stays closer to the counts.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Simple and always positive. Every element gets at least \(\gamma/(N + B\gamma)\).
  • Over-smooths large supports. The reserved mass is \((B - V)\gamma / (N + B\gamma)\), which approaches 1 when \(B\) is much larger than \(N\). Add-one smoothing is known to perform poorly for language data for this reason; prefer a small \(\gamma\) or Simple Good–Turing.
  • bins must be the support size. With the default \(B = V\), the observed elements already sum to one, and each unseen element is scored on top; see Pitfalls and Choose bins.
  • Treats all unseen elements alike, and all observed elements with the same count alike.

docs.title: freqprob.Lidstone
docs.text:
Lidstone(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, gamma: float, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Lidstone additive smoothing probability distribution.

Additive smoothing tackles the zero-probability problem by adding a virtual count gamma to every possible element before normalizing. For counts c_i, total N, and B bins, each observed element gets (c_i + gamma) / (N + B * gamma) and any unobserved element gets gamma / (N + B * gamma). This is the posterior mean under a symmetric Dirichlet prior with concentration gamma. Use it when you need a simple, principled way to keep unseen elements from scoring zero, and tune gamma to trade off between staying close to the data (small gamma) and a more uniform distribution (large gamma).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required gamma float

Additive smoothing parameter (gamma >= 0). 1.0 gives Laplace smoothing, 0.5 gives the Jeffreys prior (ELE), and gamma -> 0 approaches MLE.

required bins int | None

Total number of possible elements. If None (the default), uses the support size |V|. A larger bins reserves more mass for unseen elements.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Add-gamma smoothing gives unseen elements non-zero probability:

>>> from freqprob import Lidstone
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 3, "banana": 1}
>>> lidstone = Lidstone(freqdist, gamma=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> round(lidstone("apple"), 3)    # (3+1)/(4+2*1) = 4/6
0.667
>>> round(lidstone("banana"), 3)   # (1+1)/(4+2*1) = 2/6
0.333
>>> round(lidstone("cherry"), 3)   # 1/(4+2*1) = 1/6
0.167

A larger gamma pulls probabilities toward uniform:

>>> smooth = Lidstone(freqdist, gamma=2.0, logprob=False)
>>> smooth("apple")      # (3+2)/(4+2*2) = 5/8
0.625
>>> smooth("cherry")     # 2/(4+2*2) = 2/8
0.25

A larger bins reserves more mass for potential unseen elements:

>>> lidstone_big = Lidstone(freqdist, gamma=1.0, bins=1000, logprob=False)
>>> round(lidstone_big("apple"), 4)    # (3+1)/(4+1000) = 4/1004
0.004
>>> round(lidstone_big("unseen"), 4)   # 1/(4+1000) = 1/1004
0.001
Note

The choice of gamma is a bias-variance tradeoff: small values stay close to MLE (low bias, high variance) while large values approach a uniform distribution (higher bias, lower variance).

Initialize Lidstone smoothing.

docs.title: freqprob.Laplace
docs.text:
Laplace(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: Lidstone

Laplace (add-one) smoothing probability distribution.

The special case of Lidstone smoothing with gamma = 1.0, also called "add-one smoothing." Each observed element gets (c_i + 1) / (N + B) and any unobserved element gets 1 / (N + B) — i.e. one virtual observation added to every possible element, corresponding to a uniform Dirichlet prior. It is the most common additive smoother: reach for it when you want a simple, reasonable default that never assigns zero probability.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Total number of possible elements. If None (the default), uses the support size |V|.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Add one to every count, then normalize:

>>> from freqprob import Laplace
>>> freqdist = {"red": 3, "blue": 2, "green": 1}
>>> laplace = Laplace(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(laplace("red"), 3)     # (3+1)/(6+3) = 4/9
0.444
>>> round(laplace("blue"), 3)    # (2+1)/(6+3) = 3/9
0.333
>>> round(laplace("yellow"), 3)  # 1/(6+3) = 1/9
0.111

Initialize Laplace smoothing.

docs.title: freqprob.ELE
docs.text:
ELE(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: Lidstone

Expected Likelihood Estimation probability distribution.

The special case of Lidstone smoothing with gamma = 0.5, corresponding to the Jeffreys prior for multinomial distributions. Each observed element gets (c_i + 0.5) / (N + 0.5 * B) and any unobserved element gets 0.5 / (N + 0.5 * B) — half a virtual observation per element. This is a middle ground between MLE and Laplace: use it when add-one smoothing feels too aggressive but you still want unseen elements handled.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Total number of possible elements. If None (the default), uses the support size |V|.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Add half a count to each element, then normalize:

>>> from freqprob import ELE
>>> freqdist = {"cat": 4, "dog": 2}
>>> ele = ELE(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(ele("cat"), 3)     # (4+0.5)/(6+0.5*2) = 4.5/7
0.643
>>> round(ele("dog"), 3)     # (2+0.5)/(6+0.5*2) = 2.5/7
0.357
>>> round(ele("bird"), 3)    # 0.5/(6+0.5*2) = 0.5/7
0.071
Note

ELE applies less smoothing than Laplace (gamma = 1), so it stays closer to the observed frequencies while still avoiding zero probabilities.

Initialize Expected Likelihood Estimation.

docs.title: freqprob.Bayesian
docs.text:
Bayesian(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, alpha: float = 1.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Bayesian smoothing with a Dirichlet prior.

Estimates probabilities as the posterior mean under a symmetric Dirichlet prior, adding alpha pseudocounts to each possible outcome. Each observed element gets (c_i + alpha) / (N + V * alpha) and any unobserved element gets alpha / (N + V * alpha), where N is the total count and V the support size. This is numerically identical to Lidstone smoothing with gamma = alpha, but framed so that alpha reads as prior belief: use it when you want a theoretically principled smoother whose strength you can tune from near-MLE (small alpha) to strongly uniform (large alpha).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required alpha float

Dirichlet concentration parameter (alpha > 0). alpha -> 0 approaches MLE, alpha = 1 gives a uniform prior (Laplace smoothing), and alpha > 1 prefers more uniform distributions. Defaults to 1.0.

1.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Bayesian smoothing with a uniform prior (alpha = 1):

>>> from freqprob import Bayesian
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 8, "banana": 4, "cherry": 1}
>>> bayes = Bayesian(freqdist, alpha=1.0, logprob=False)
>>> bayes("apple")     # (8+1)/(13+3*1) = 9/16
0.5625
>>> bayes("banana")    # (4+1)/(13+3*1) = 5/16
0.3125
>>> bayes("unseen")    # 1/(13+3*1) = 1/16
0.0625

A larger alpha smooths more strongly toward uniform:

>>> bayes_smooth = Bayesian(freqdist, alpha=2.0, logprob=False)
>>> round(bayes_smooth("apple"), 3)    # (8+2)/(13+3*2) = 10/19
0.526
>>> round(bayes_smooth("unseen"), 3)   # 2/(13+3*2) = 2/19
0.105

A small alpha stays closer to the observed frequencies:

>>> bayes_minimal = Bayesian(freqdist, alpha=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> round(bayes_minimal("apple"), 3)   # (8+0.1)/(13+3*0.1) = 8.1/13.3
0.609
Note

A positive alpha is required; passing alpha <= 0 raises ValueError. Equivalent to Lidstone with gamma = alpha.

docs.text: • Laplace (1814); Lidstone (1920); Manning & Schütze (1999, §6.2); MacKay & Peto (1995) for the Dirichlet view. See References.

docs.title: Katz and Stupid back-off
docs.text:
KatzBackoff, StupidBackoff · n-gram back-off · bigram input

Back-off models use the bigram estimate when the bigram has been seen, and fall back ("back off") to the unigram model when it has not. Katz (1987) discounts the observed counts with Good–Turing and normalizes the back-off, so the result is a probability distribution. Stupid Back-off (Brants et al., 2007) skips the discounting and normalization, which makes it very cheap at web scale, but its scores are not probabilities.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a bigram \((v, w)\) with count \(c = c(v, w)\) and context total \(c(v)\), Katz back-off gives

\[ P(w \mid v) = \begin{cases} d_c\,\dfrac{c}{c(v)} & \text{if } c > 0,\\[1ex] \alpha(v)\,P_{\text{uni}}(w) & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \]

where \(d_c\) is the Good–Turing discount ratio for counts \(1 \leq c \leq k\) (\(d_c = 1\) above \(k\)) and \(\alpha(v)\) makes each context's distribution sum to one. Stupid Back-off scores

\[ S(w \mid v) = \begin{cases} c / c(v) & \text{if } c > 0,\\ \alpha\,P_{\text{uni}}(w) & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \]

with a fixed \(\alpha\) = alpha, 0.4 by default.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Katz back-off needs a spread of low counts to estimate its discounts:

>>> import freqprob
>>> bigrams = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 4,
...     ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 2,
...     ("my", "cat"): 1,
...     ("my", "dog"): 1,
...     ("my", "bird"): 1,
...     ("his", "fish"): 1,
...     ("her", "fish"): 1,
...     ("its", "bird"): 1,
... }
>>> katz = freqprob.KatzBackoff(bigrams, logprob=False)
>>> [round(katz(b), 3) for b in [("the", "cat"), ("my", "cat"), ("my", "fish")]]
[0.571, 0.222, 0.333]
>>> sb = freqprob.StupidBackoff(bigrams, logprob=False)
>>> [round(sb(b), 3) for b in [("the", "cat"), ("my", "cat"), ("my", "fish")]]
[0.571, 0.333, 0.047]

Under Katz back-off, the singletons after "my" are discounted from \(1/3\) to \(0.222\), and the freed mass goes to unseen words such as "fish". Stupid Back-off leaves the observed scores alone and scores "fish" after "my" as \(0.4 \times P_{\text{uni}}(\text{fish}) = 0.4 \times 2/17\).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Katz is normalized; Stupid Back-off is not, so its scores are for ranking and not for perplexity (see Pitfalls).
  • Katz needs varied low counts. With too few distinct counts, some discounts default to 1, leaving little mass for unseen bigrams.
  • Bigrams only. Keys must be (context, word) pairs.

docs.title: freqprob.KatzBackoff
docs.text:
KatzBackoff(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, k: int = 5, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Katz back-off bigram smoothing.

Katz's method discounts observed bigram counts with Good-Turing and redistributes the freed mass to a lower-order unigram model through normalized back-off weights. Following Katz (1987), only counts up to a threshold k are discounted (counts above k are assumed reliable). For a bigram (context, word) with count c and context total C,

P(word | context) = d_c * c / C if c > 0,

P(word | context) = alpha(context) * P_uni(word) otherwise,

where d_c is the Good-Turing discount ratio for count c and alpha(context) is chosen so each context's distribution sums to one. It is one of the classic n-gram smoothing methods and pairs naturally with freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring, which uses the same count-of-counts machinery.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required k int

Good-Turing discounting is applied to counts 1 <= c <= k; larger counts are left undiscounted. Defaults to 5.

5 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Reliable (high) counts are barely discounted, rare counts are discounted more, and unseen bigrams back off to the unigram model:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 4, ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2, ("a", "dog"): 2,
...     ("my", "cat"): 1, ("my", "dog"): 1, ("my", "bird"): 1,
...     ("his", "fish"): 1, ("her", "fish"): 1, ("its", "bird"): 1,
... }
>>> katz = KatzBackoff(bigram_counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(katz(("the", "cat")), 3)    # reliable count, undiscounted
0.571
>>> round(katz(("my", "cat")), 3)     # singleton, Good-Turing discounted
0.222
>>> round(katz(("my", "fish")), 3)    # unseen in context, backs off
0.333
Note

This implementation assumes bigram input. Good-Turing discounting needs a spread of low counts (singletons, doubletons, ...) to estimate discounts; with too few distinct counts some discounts default to 1 (no discounting), leaving little or no mass for unseen bigrams.

Initialize Katz back-off smoothing.

docs.title: freqprob.StupidBackoff
docs.text:
StupidBackoff(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, alpha: float = 0.4, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Stupid Back-off bigram scoring.

A deliberately simple, unnormalized scheme introduced by Brants et al. (2007) for web-scale language modeling. An observed bigram scores its relative frequency; an unseen bigram scores a fixed weight alpha times the lower-order unigram score:

S(word | context) = c(context, word) / c(context) if observed,

S(word | context) = alpha * P_uni(word) otherwise.

Because it skips the normalization Katz back-off performs, the scores do not form a probability distribution (they do not sum to one), but they are very cheap to compute and work well for ranking when data is plentiful.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping (context, word) bigrams to counts. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required alpha float

Back-off weight applied when falling back to the unigram model. Defaults to 0.4 (the value recommended by Brants et al.).

0.4 logprob bool

Return log-scores if True (the default), otherwise plain scores.

True

Examples:

Observed bigrams score their relative frequency; unseen bigrams are penalized by alpha and scored from the unigram model:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> sb = StupidBackoff(bigram_counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(sb(("the", "cat")), 3)      # 5 / 8
0.625
>>> round(sb(("a", "dog")), 3)        # 1 / 3
0.333
>>> round(sb(("big", "dog")), 3)      # 0.4 * P_uni("dog")
0.154
Note

Stupid Back-off returns scores, not normalized probabilities, so metrics that assume a valid distribution (such as perplexity) are not meaningful here. Use it for ranking and comparison, where only the relative ordering of scores matters.

docs.title: Baselines: MLE, Uniform, Random
docs.text:
MLE, Uniform, Random · no smoothing · reference points

These three estimators are the reference points against which smoothing is judged. MLE uses the counts as they are, Uniform ignores them, and Random replaces them with random ones.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The maximum-likelihood estimate is the relative frequency:

\[ P_{\text{MLE}}(w) = (1 - p_0)\,\frac{c(w)}{N}, \qquad P_{\text{MLE}}(\text{unseen}) = p_0, \]

with \(p_0\) = unobs_prob, 0 by default. Uniform gives every observed element \((1 - p_0)/V\), whatever its count. Random draws a random count between the smallest and largest observed counts for each element, and normalizes those like MLE; seed makes it reproducible.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example counts:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> mle = freqprob.MLE(counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(mle("the"), 4), round(mle("dog"), 4), mle("zebra")
(0.3333, 0.0333, 0.0)
>>> freqprob.Uniform(counts, logprob=False)("the")
0.1
>>> random = freqprob.Random(counts, seed=0, logprob=False)
>>> round(sum(random(w) for w in counts), 6)
1.0

Reserving mass with unobs_prob rescales the observed elements:

>>> mle = freqprob.MLE(counts, unobs_prob=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> round(mle("the"), 4), mle("zebra")
(0.3, 0.1)

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• MLE is unbiased for the observed elements and gives nothing to the rest, which makes it unsuitable whenever unseen elements can occur.
  • unobs_prob is a per-element score: every unseen element receives \(p_0\) (see Pitfalls).
  • Uniform and Random are controls. A smoothing method that does no better than them on held-out data is not using the counts well.

docs.title: freqprob.MLE
docs.text:
MLE(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

Estimates each element's probability as its relative frequency in the observed data — the most intuitive baseline. For counts c_i with total N, each observed element gets (1 - p0) * c_i / N and any unobserved element gets the reserved mass p0 (0.0 by default, i.e. unseen elements score zero).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass p0 for unobserved elements (0.0 <= p0 <= 1.0). Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Probabilities are relative frequencies; unseen elements score zero:

>>> mle = MLE({"apple": 6, "banana": 3, "cherry": 1}, logprob=False)
>>> mle("apple")
0.6
>>> mle("banana")
0.3
>>> mle("unknown")
0.0

Reserving mass for unseen elements rescales the observed ones:

>>> smoothed = MLE({"apple": 6, "banana": 3, "cherry": 1},
...                unobs_prob=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> round(smoothed("apple"), 3)
0.54
>>> smoothed("unknown")
0.1
Note

MLE underlies most smoothing methods but assigns zero probability to unseen events, which is problematic for sparse data. Prefer Laplace, Lidstone, or a more advanced method when unseen elements are likely.

docs.title: freqprob.Uniform
docs.text:
Uniform(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Uniform probability distribution.

The simplest baseline: assign equal probability to every observed element, ignoring the counts entirely. Useful as a non-informative prior or as a reference point when comparing smoothing methods.

For a vocabulary of size V with reserved mass p0, each observed element gets (1 - p0) / V and any unobserved element gets p0.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts. The counts are ignored; only the number of distinct elements matters.

required unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass p0 for unobserved elements (0.0 <= p0 <= 1.0). Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Counts are ignored, so both observed elements score the same:

>>> uniform = Uniform({"apple": 10, "banana": 1}, unobs_prob=0.1, logprob=False)
>>> uniform("apple")
0.45
>>> uniform("banana")
0.45
>>> uniform("cherry")  # unobserved
0.1
Note

Because it discards frequency information, Uniform is meant as a baseline. Use MLE, Lidstone, or Laplace when counts should matter.

docs.title: freqprob.Random
docs.text:
Random(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True, seed: int | None = None)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Random probability distribution.

Assigns pseudo-random probabilities, useful for testing and as a randomized baseline. Each element is given a random count drawn from the observed count range, and those counts are then normalized like MLE. A fixed seed makes the result reproducible.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts. Only the min/max counts are used, to bound the random counts.

required unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass for unobserved elements. Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True seed int | None

Seed for the random number generator, for reproducible results. Defaults to None.

None

Examples:

The probabilities are random but form a valid distribution, and a fixed seed is reproducible:

>>> freqdist = {"apple": 5, "banana": 2, "cherry": 8}
>>> a = Random(freqdist, seed=123, logprob=False)
>>> b = Random(freqdist, seed=123, logprob=False)
>>> a("apple") == b("apple")
True
>>> round(sum(a(e) for e in freqdist), 6)
1.0
Note

Primarily for testing, debugging, and providing a randomized baseline for comparison. It is not a smoothing method in any meaningful sense.

docs.title: Certainty degree
docs.text:
CertaintyDegree · experimental

Experimental

CertaintyDegree is an estimator under development, without a published reference. It is documented for completeness; do not use it as your only or main estimator yet.

The certainty degree reserves mass for unseen elements according to how plausible it is that the sample has already covered the support.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(N\) observations of \(V\) distinct elements and a support of \(B\) elements (bins, \(V\) by default), the mass reserved for unseen elements is

\[ p_0 = \max\!\Big(\big(\tfrac{V}{B + 1}\big)^{N},\ \texttt{unobs\_prob}\Big), \]

the probability that \(N\) draws from \(B + 1\) equally likely elements all fall among the \(V\) observed ones. The observed elements share the rest in proportion to their counts, \(P(w) = (1 - p_0)\,c(w)/N\), and each unseen element scores \(p_0\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example counts:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> cd = freqprob.CertaintyDegree(counts, logprob=False)
>>> [round(cd(w), 4) for w in ("the", "dog", "zebra")]
[0.3142, 0.0314, 0.0573]
>>> round(freqprob.CertaintyDegree(counts, bins=100, logprob=False)("zebra"), 6)
0.0

With the default support, \(p_0 = (10/11)^{30} \approx 0.057\). Declaring a support of 100 elements makes \(p_0\) vanish: if the 30 observations had been spread over 101 equally likely elements, finding only ten of them would be very unlikely.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Shrinks quickly with \(N\): the reserved mass falls exponentially with the number of observations.
  • A larger bins reserves less mass, unlike the additive methods, because it makes the observed concentration on few elements more telling.
  • The unseen score is per element, as for unobs_prob in MLE (see Pitfalls).

docs.title: freqprob.CertaintyDegree
docs.text:
CertaintyDegree(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, unobs_prob: Probability = 0.0, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Certainty-degree smoothing.

Reserves probability mass for unseen elements based on the degree of certainty that no unobserved samples remain, derived from the number of observations relative to the support size. As more of the possible bins are observed, the reserved mass shrinks; the remaining mass rescales the Maximum-Likelihood estimate of each observed element.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Optional total number of possible sample bins for the experiment. If None (the default), it defaults to the number of observed types.

None unobs_prob Probability

Reserved probability mass for unobserved states (0.0 <= unobs_prob <= 1.0). Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities. Counts are corrected to avoid domain errors when taking logarithms.

True

Examples:

Observed elements are rescaled by the computed certainty mass, and the remainder is reserved for unseen elements:

>>> from freqprob import CertaintyDegree
>>> freqdist = {"apple": 8, "banana": 4, "cherry": 2, "date": 1}
>>> cd = CertaintyDegree(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(cd("apple"), 3)
0.515
>>> round(cd("date"), 3)
0.064
>>> round(cd("kiwi"), 3)  # unobserved
0.035
Note

This is an experimental distribution under development by Tiago Tresoldi; it should not be used as the sole or main distribution yet.

docs.title: Interpolation: Interpolated and Jelinek–Mercer
docs.text:
Interpolated, JelinekMercer · linear interpolation

Interpolation mixes a specific model with a general one: a trigram model with a bigram model, say, or a small in-domain sample with a large background corpus. The specific model is sharper where it has evidence; the general model covers what it has not seen. Jelinek and Mercer (1980) fit the mixing weight on held-out data.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(P_{\text{high}}\) and \(P_{\text{low}}\) the relative frequencies of the two distributions and \(\lambda\) = lambda_weight,

\[ P(w) = \lambda\,P_{\text{high}}(w) + (1 - \lambda)\,P_{\text{low}}(\operatorname{ctx}(w)). \]

When the high-order keys are longer tuples than the low-order ones, the low-order key is the suffix of the high-order n-gram: bigram \((w_2, w_3)\) for trigram \((w_1, w_2, w_3)\). When both have the same type of key, keys are matched directly. JelinekMercer estimates \(\lambda\) by expectation–maximization on a held-out distribution (held_out_dist), maximizing its likelihood; without held-out data it uses lambda_weight.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
>>> import freqprob
>>> trigrams = {("the", "big", "cat"): 3, ("a", "big", "dog"): 2}
>>> bigrams = {("big", "cat"): 5, ("big", "dog"): 3, ("small", "cat"): 2}
>>> interp = freqprob.Interpolated(trigrams, bigrams, lambda_weight=0.7, logprob=False)
>>> round(interp(("the", "big", "cat")), 3)  # 0.7 * 3/5 + 0.3 * 5/10
0.57
>>> round(interp(("one", "big", "cat")), 3)  # unseen trigram: 0.3 * 5/10
0.15
>>> held_out = {("the", "big", "cat"): 8, ("a", "big", "dog"): 6}
>>> jm = freqprob.JelinekMercer(trigrams, bigrams, held_out_dist=held_out, logprob=False)
>>> jm.estimated_lambda > 0.5
True

The held-out data repeats the trigrams the high-order model already knows, so EM moves the weight towards it.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Keeps specificity and coverage: unseen high-order n-grams still get the low-order mass.
  • The weight matters. Tune it on held-out data, which JelinekMercer does for you; the held-out data must be disjoint from the training data.
  • One global weight. The original scheme uses weights per context bucket; JelinekMercer fits a single \(\lambda\).
  • Relative frequencies on both levels. To smooth each level as well, combine a smoothed estimator's scores yourself.

docs.title: freqprob.Interpolated
docs.text:
Interpolated(high_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, low_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, lambda_weight: float = 0.7, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Linear interpolation smoothing between two frequency distributions.

Blends a higher-order distribution with a lower-order one using a weighted average, lambda_weight * P_high + (1 - lambda_weight) * P_low. This keeps the specificity of the high-order model while borrowing robustness from the smoother low-order model. Two modes are detected automatically from the keys:

  • N-gram interpolation, when the high-order keys are longer tuples than the low-order keys. The lower-order context is taken as the suffix of each high-order n-gram (e.g. bigram (w2, w3) from trigram (w1, w2, w3)).
  • Same-type interpolation, when both distributions share the same key type (strings or equal-length tuples). Keys are matched directly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default high_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Higher-order frequency distribution mapping elements to counts (e.g. trigrams). For n-gram mode its tuple keys must be at least as long as those of low_order_dist.

required low_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Lower-order frequency distribution (e.g. bigrams).

required lambda_weight float

Interpolation weight 0 <= lambda_weight <= 1 for the high-order model. Higher values favor specificity, lower values favor smoothing. Defaults to 0.7.

0.7 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

N-gram interpolation (trigrams backed off to bigrams). The score of ('the', 'big', 'cat') is 0.7 * (3/5) + 0.3 * (5/10), and an unseen trigram backs off to 0.3 * (5/10):

>>> trigrams = {("the", "big", "cat"): 3, ("a", "big", "dog"): 2}
>>> bigrams = {("big", "cat"): 5, ("big", "dog"): 3, ("small", "cat"): 2}
>>> interp = Interpolated(trigrams, bigrams, lambda_weight=0.7, logprob=False)
>>> round(interp(("the", "big", "cat")), 3)
0.57
>>> round(interp(("unseen", "big", "cat")), 3)
0.15

Same-type interpolation between two string distributions. The score of "word1" is 0.6 * (10/15) + 0.4 * (3/10):

>>> model1 = {"word1": 10, "word2": 5}
>>> model2 = {"word1": 3, "word3": 7}
>>> interp = Interpolated(model1, model2, lambda_weight=0.6, logprob=False)
>>> round(interp("word1"), 3)
0.52
>>> round(interp("word2"), 3)
0.2
>>> round(interp("word3"), 3)
0.28
Note

The mode is inferred from the key types, so mixed tuple lengths within a single distribution raise an error. Unseen high-order n-grams back off to the low-order model, and all probabilities are floored at 1e-10 for numerical stability. The weight lambda_weight is best tuned on held-out data.

docs.title: freqprob.JelinekMercer
docs.text:
JelinekMercer(high_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, low_order_dist: FrequencyDistribution, held_out_dist: FrequencyDistribution | None = None, lambda_weight: float = 0.5, em_iterations: int = 10, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: Interpolated

Jelinek-Mercer smoothing with an EM-estimated interpolation weight.

Jelinek-Mercer smoothing linearly interpolates a higher-order model with a lower-order one, exactly as Interpolated does, but chooses the interpolation weight lambda by deleted interpolation: given a held-out distribution, the weight is fitted with the Expectation-Maximization algorithm to maximize the likelihood of that held-out data. Without held-out data it behaves as fixed-weight interpolation using lambda_weight.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default high_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Higher-order frequency distribution (e.g. trigrams).

required low_order_dist FrequencyDistribution

Lower-order frequency distribution (e.g. bigrams).

required held_out_dist FrequencyDistribution | None

Optional held-out frequency distribution used to fit lambda by EM. If None (the default), the supplied lambda_weight is used unchanged.

None lambda_weight float

Interpolation weight 0 <= lambda_weight <= 1 for the high-order model. Used directly when there is no held-out data, and as the EM starting point otherwise. Defaults to 0.5.

0.5 em_iterations int

Number of EM iterations when fitting lambda from held-out data (a positive integer). Defaults to 10.

10 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Attributes:

Name Type Description estimated_lambda

The interpolation weight actually used — either the EM-fitted value or lambda_weight when no held-out data was given.

Examples:

With no held-out data the estimated weight is exactly lambda_weight, and scoring matches fixed-weight interpolation:

>>> trigrams = {("the", "big", "cat"): 3, ("a", "big", "dog"): 2}
>>> bigrams = {("big", "cat"): 5, ("big", "dog"): 3}
>>> jm = JelinekMercer(trigrams, bigrams, lambda_weight=0.6, logprob=False)
>>> round(jm.estimated_lambda, 2)
0.6
>>> round(jm(("the", "big", "cat")), 3)   # 0.6 * (3/5) + 0.4 * (5/8)
0.61

Held-out data that the high-order model predicts well pulls the weight up:

>>> held_out = {("the", "big", "cat"): 8, ("a", "big", "dog"): 6}
>>> jm = JelinekMercer(trigrams, bigrams, held_out_dist=held_out, logprob=False)
>>> jm.estimated_lambda > 0.5
True
Note

EM fits a single global lambda (not the per-context bucketed weights of the original Jelinek-Mercer scheme). The held-out data should be disjoint from the training data for the estimate to be meaningful.

docs.title: Kneser–Ney
docs.text:
KneserNey, ModifiedKneserNey · n-gram smoothing · bigram input

Kneser–Ney smoothing (Kneser & Ney, 1995) is the standard classical method for n-gram language models. It discounts every observed bigram by a fixed amount, and gives the freed mass to a lower-order model in which a word's weight is the number of distinct contexts it follows, not its frequency. A word that is frequent but appears in only one context ("Francisco", nearly always after "San") is then unlikely in a new context. Modified Kneser–Ney (Chen & Goodman, 1999) uses three discounts instead of one.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a bigram \((v, w)\) with count \(c(v, w)\), context total \(c(v)\) and discount \(d\),

\[ P(w \mid v) = \frac{\max\big(c(v, w) - d,\ 0\big)}{c(v)} + \lambda(v)\,P_{\text{cont}}(w), \qquad \lambda(v) = \frac{d\,N_{1+}(v)}{c(v)}, \]

where \(N_{1+}(v)\) is the number of distinct words seen after \(v\), and the continuation probability is

\[ P_{\text{cont}}(w) = \frac{|\{v : c(v, w) > 0\}|}{|\{(v', w') : c(v', w') > 0\}|}. \]

An unseen context backs off to \(P_{\text{cont}}(w)\) alone. ModifiedKneserNey uses discounts \(d_1\), \(d_2\) and \(d_{3+}\) for bigrams seen once, twice and three or more times, estimated from the counts of counts.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example bigrams:

>>> import freqprob
>>> bigrams = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5,
...     ("the", "dog"): 3,
...     ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1,
...     ("big", "cat"): 1,
...     ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> kn = freqprob.KneserNey(bigrams, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> [round(kn(b), 3) for b in [("the", "cat"), ("the", "dog"), ("big", "dog"), ("new", "cat")]]
[0.625, 0.375, 0.375, 0.5]
>>> mkn = freqprob.ModifiedKneserNey(bigrams, logprob=False)
>>> [round(mkn(b), 3) for b in [("the", "cat"), ("a", "cat"), ("big", "dog")]]
[0.625, 0.558, 0.3]

"cat" and "dog" each follow three distinct contexts, so their continuation probabilities are equal (0.5), and a new context gives them the same probability although "cat" is more frequent. "big" was followed only by "cat", so "dog" after "big" gets the context's whole back-off weight, \(0.75 \times 0.5 = 0.375\).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• The strongest classical n-gram smoother, especially in its modified form (Chen & Goodman, 1999).
  • Normalized: the probabilities of the words after each context sum to one.
  • Bigrams only. Keys must be (context, word) pairs; other keys are ignored. A word never seen in any bigram scores 0 (the floor, in log space).
  • The discount is typically between 0.5 and 0.8; 0.75 is a robust default. ModifiedKneserNey estimates its discounts and needs enough variety in the counts to do so.

docs.title: freqprob.KneserNey
docs.text:
KneserNey(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, discount: float = 0.75, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Kneser-Ney smoothing probability distribution.

One of the most effective smoothing methods for language modeling. It combines absolute discounting with interpolation and, crucially, weights a word by the diversity of contexts it appears in (its continuation probability) rather than its raw frequency. Each observed bigram scores max(c - d, 0) / c(context) + backoff(context) * P_cont(word), and an unseen bigram backs off to backoff(context) * P_cont(word).

This is absolute discounting with the unigram model replaced by the continuation distribution, and it shares the back-off machinery with freqprob.AbsoluteDiscounting accordingly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping bigrams to their observed counts, in the form {(context, word): count}. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required discount float

Absolute discounting parameter 0 < d < 1. Common values are 0.5-0.8. Defaults to 0.75.

0.75 logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

Observed bigrams are discounted and interpolated with the continuation model, while unseen bigrams back off to it through the context's back-off weight:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> kn = KneserNey(bigram_counts, discount=0.75, logprob=False)
>>> round(kn(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.625

An unseen bigram whose word is known scores through the context's back-off weight rather than a flat average -- here 0.75 * P_cont(dog), since big was only ever followed by one word:

>>> round(kn(("big", "dog")), 3)
0.375

An unseen context falls back to the continuation probability alone:

>>> round(kn(("new_context", "cat")), 3)
0.5
Note

This implementation assumes bigram input. The discount d is typically between 0.5 and 0.8; 0.75 is a robust default. Reliable continuation probabilities require sufficient bigram data. A word that never appears in the data has no continuation probability, so it scores at the floor rather than borrowing an average.

Initialize Kneser-Ney smoothing.

docs.title: freqprob.ModifiedKneserNey
docs.text:
ModifiedKneserNey(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: BigramBackoff

Modified Kneser-Ney smoothing probability distribution.

An enhanced Kneser-Ney variant that applies a different discount depending on a bigram's count: d1 for singletons, d2 for doubletons, and d3 for counts of three or more. Those discounts are estimated automatically from the data's count-of-counts statistics, which usually makes it more accurate than the fixed-discount version.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Frequency distribution mapping bigrams to their observed counts, in the form {(context, word): count}. Non-bigram keys are ignored.

required logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities.

True

Examples:

The discount adapts to each bigram's count, and the score interpolates the discounted estimate with the continuation model:

>>> bigram_counts = {
...     ("the", "cat"): 5, ("the", "dog"): 3, ("a", "cat"): 2,
...     ("a", "dog"): 1, ("big", "cat"): 1, ("small", "dog"): 1,
... }
>>> mkn = ModifiedKneserNey(bigram_counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(mkn(("the", "cat")), 3)
0.625
>>> round(mkn(("a", "cat")), 3)
0.558
Note

Modified Kneser-Ney is a standard, state-of-the-art classical smoothing method for n-gram language models. Because it estimates its discounts from the data, it is more robust than fixed-discount methods but needs enough varied counts to estimate them reliably.

docs.title: Simple Good–Turing
docs.text:
SimpleGoodTuring · discounting · estimates the unseen mass from the singletons

Good–Turing estimation (Good, 1953, after Turing) uses the frequencies of frequencies to decide how much probability belongs to elements not seen. Its central insight is that the mass of everything unseen is estimated by the share of observations that are singletons. Gale and Sampson's (1995) "simple" version smooths the frequencies of frequencies with a log-linear fit, which makes it practical for real data.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(N_r\) be the number of elements seen exactly \(r\) times. The total mass reserved for unseen elements is

\[ p_0 = \frac{N_1}{N}, \]

and an element seen \(r\) times is given the adjusted count

\[ r^* = (r + 1)\,\frac{S(N_{r+1})}{S(N_r)}, \]

where \(S\) is the log-linear smoothing of \(N_r\). For small \(r\), the empirical Turing estimate (\(S(N_r) = N_r\)) is used for as long as it differs significantly from the smoothed one, at the level p_value. The adjusted counts are renormalized so that the observed elements share \(1 - p_0\).

An unseen element is given \(p_0 / (B - V)\). The support size \(B\) = bins defaults to \(V + N_1\): as many unseen elements as singletons. total_unseen_mass reports \(p_0\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example counts, four of the 30 observations are singletons:

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> sgt = freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring(counts, logprob=False)
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 4)  # N1 / N = 4 / 30
0.1333
>>> [round(sgt(w), 4) for w in ("the", "dog", "zebra")]
[0.3066, 0.0247, 0.0333]

The four default unseen elements share \(0.133\), so each gets \(0.033\). Each singleton gives up a quarter of its relative frequency (\(0.033 \to 0.025\)), while the most frequent word gives up less (\(0.333 \to 0.307\)).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Principled unseen mass. \(N_1/N\) is a direct estimate of the probability that the next observation is new, which is what most applications need.
  • Discounts rare elements most. High counts are reliable and barely adjusted.
  • Needs a spread of low counts. The log-linear fit needs several distinct values of \(r\), and the method assumes singletons are present. By default it proceeds when these assumptions fail; allow_fail=False raises a RuntimeWarning instead. With no singletons, \(p_0\) is default_p0, or \(1/(N + 1)\) if that is not given.
  • bins only shares the unseen mass out. It does not change \(p_0\); pass the true support size when it is known.
  • The same estimate of the unseen mass underlies sample_coverage.

docs.title: freqprob.SimpleGoodTuring
docs.text:
SimpleGoodTuring(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, p_value: float = 0.05, default_p0: float | None = None, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True, allow_fail: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Simple Good-Turing smoothing.

Reestimates counts using the frequency of frequencies (how many elements were seen once, twice, and so on), fitting a log-linear model to smooth the tail so that mass can be reserved for unseen elements. This is the practical Gale-Sampson formulation of the Good-Turing method originally developed by Turing and Good, and is a strong general-purpose smoother when the data show a spread of low-frequency counts (many singletons, fewer doubletons, etc.).

This implementation follows those by "maxbane" (2011, https://github.com/maxbane/simplegoodturing/blob/master/sgt.py), Geoffrey Sampson's original C code (1995-2008, https://www.grsampson.net/Resources.html), and the NLTK project (Loper, Bird et al., 2001-2018). Because of minor differences intended to guarantee non-zero probabilities under expected underflow, the reliance on scipy, and the handling of probabilities that are not computable when SGT assumptions are not met, most results will not exactly match the Gale-Sampson "gold standard", though the differences are never expected to be significant.

Note

Since v0.4.0, unseen queries return the per-word probability p0 / (bins - V) rather than the total mass p0, making the method compatible with perplexity calculations and consistent with the other smoothers. Use the total_unseen_mass property to recover p0 (the total mass for all unseen words combined).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required p_value float

The p-value for the confidence interval of the empirical Turing estimate, guiding the choice between the Turing estimate x and the log-linear smoothed value y. Defaults to 0.05 (Sampson's reference implementation), though the authors suggest 0.1.

0.05 default_p0 float | None

Optional probability for unobserved samples (p0) used when no single-count samples are observed. If unspecified, p0 defaults to a Laplace estimate for the current distribution — an intended change from the Gale-Sampson reference.

None bins int | None

Total support size for computing per-word unseen probabilities. If None (the default), uses the heuristic bins = V_observed + N1 where N1 is the number of singletons, assuming about as many unseen types as singletons. Pass an exact support size if known.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities. Counts are corrected to avoid domain errors when taking logarithms.

True allow_fail bool

If True (the default), estimation proceeds even when the essential SGT assumptions are not met (log-linear regression slope > -1.0, or an unobserved count reached before crossing the smoothing threshold), and may yield an unreliable distribution. If False, raise RuntimeWarning in those cases.

True

Examples:

SGT needs a spread of low-frequency counts, so use a Zipfian-ish distribution with several singletons. Observed elements are discounted and unseen elements receive a share of the reserved mass:

>>> from freqprob import SimpleGoodTuring
>>> freqdist = {"a": 10, "b": 5, "c": 4, "d": 3, "e": 2,
...             "f": 2, "g": 1, "h": 1, "i": 1, "j": 1}
>>> sgt = SimpleGoodTuring(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(float(sgt("a")), 3)
0.307
>>> round(float(sgt("g")), 3)  # a singleton
0.025
>>> round(sgt("unknown"), 3)  # per-word unseen probability
0.033
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 3)  # total mass for all unseen words
0.133

Initialize Simple Good-Turing smoothing.

docs.title: total_unseen_mass property
docs.text:
total_unseen_mass: float

Total probability mass reserved for ALL unseen words (p0).

This is the value that Good-Turing actually estimates. The per-word unseen probability returned by __call__() is this value divided by the estimated number of unseen types (bins - V_observed).

Returns:

Type Description float

Total probability mass for all unseen words combined.

Examples:

>>> from freqprob import SimpleGoodTuring
>>> freqdist = {"a": 10, "b": 5, "c": 1, "d": 1, "e": 1}
>>> sgt = SimpleGoodTuring(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(sgt.total_unseen_mass, 3)  # total mass for all unseen words
0.167
>>> round(sgt("unknown"), 3)  # per-word probability for one unseen word
0.056

docs.title: Witten–Bell
docs.text:
WittenBell · discounting · estimates the unseen mass from the number of types

Witten–Bell smoothing (Witten & Bell, 1991) reserves mass for unseen elements in proportion to how often a new element has been observed: each of the \(V\) distinct elements was new once, out of \(N + V\) events of "seeing an element" or "seeing a new element". It has no parameters beyond the support size.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[ P(w) = \frac{c(w)}{N + V}, \qquad p_0 = \frac{V}{N + V}, \qquad P(\text{unseen}) = \frac{p_0}{B - V}, \]

where \(B\) = bins. With the default (bins unset, or equal to \(V\)), the whole reserved mass goes to a single unseen bin, so every unseen element scores \(p_0\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example counts, \(V = 10\) and \(N = 30\):

>>> import freqprob
>>> counts = dict(the=10, cat=5, sat=4, on=3, mat=2, a=2, dog=1, ran=1, far=1, away=1)
>>> wb = freqprob.WittenBell(counts, bins=100, logprob=False)
>>> [round(wb(w), 4) for w in ("the", "dog", "zebra")]
[0.25, 0.025, 0.0028]

The observed words keep \(30/40\) of the mass, and the 90 unseen words share the remaining \(10/40\).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Parameter-free and assumption-light. It needs no fit, so it works where Simple Good–Turing's assumptions fail.
  • Discounts all observed elements by the same factor, \(N/(N + V)\), unlike Good–Turing, which discounts rare elements more.
  • Reserves more mass when the vocabulary grows quickly: a sample in which most observations are new types predicts more new types.
  • Pass bins to share the unseen mass among the possible elements; see Pitfalls.

docs.title: freqprob.WittenBell
docs.text:
WittenBell(freqdist: FrequencyDistribution, bins: int | None = None, logprob: bool = True)

Bases: ScoringMethod

Witten-Bell smoothing.

Reserves probability mass for unseen elements based on how many distinct types were observed, treating each new type as evidence that more unseen types exist. The reserved mass is T / (N + T), where T is the number of observed types and N the total number of observations; the remaining mass is discounted proportionally so all estimates sum to one:

  • p = T / (Z * (N + T)) for an unobserved element, and
  • p = c / (N + T) for an element observed c times.

Useful as a lightweight discounting method when a simple, parameter-free way to handle unseen elements is needed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freqdist FrequencyDistribution

Mapping of elements to observed counts.

required bins int | None

Optional total number of possible sample bins for the experiment. If None (the default), it defaults to the number of observed types, so the full reserved mass is assigned to a single unseen bin.

None logprob bool

Return log-probabilities if True (the default), otherwise plain probabilities. Counts are corrected to avoid domain errors when taking logarithms.

True

Examples:

Observed elements are scored by relative frequency over N + T, and unseen elements share the reserved mass:

>>> from freqprob import WittenBell
>>> freqdist = {"the": 100, "a": 50, "cat": 3, "dog": 2, "rare": 1}
>>> wb = WittenBell(freqdist, logprob=False)
>>> round(wb("the"), 3)
0.621
>>> round(wb("rare"), 3)
0.006
>>> round(wb("unicorn"), 3)  # unobserved
0.031
